strings.USA_ICE_prepare_intervention_tt: With the developments in Iceland souring our reputation, we will need to take action to defend the opinion of the OFN abroad.
strings.USA_Greenland_flag_tt: Hoisting our flag, the Greenlandic people finally have a banner to rally under.
strings.USA_arise_Greenland_tt: It's dawn in Greenland, our ancient land.
strings.USA_IND.1.d:
Previous Democratic administrations had been perfectly fine with Nehru's non-alignment. After all, Castro had been the same way, and López Mateos. Even if they didn't want to be part of the OFN for whatever reason, and wouldn't stop trading with the Sphere, they were still trusty anti-fascist allies.

Now, it's not that Nixon was completely against non-alignment as an idea. He understood the concept perfectly - hell, he even understood why they'd do it. They wanted to buy domestic, play both sides off safely for the best deal, knowing that because they weren't superpowers, it was the best bet. It was respectable, and Nixon personally just considered it their way of business - and in good times, soft times, that was all well and good.

But these were hard times. And Nixon wanted Mr. Nehru and his socialist buddies to understand that if they were going to tell Japan to back off, they had to get closer to the US. They could keep their non-alignment, be neutralists as they liked, but the two democracies could accomplish so much together - and it started by seeing American aid as the gift it was and not treating it like some puppet's strings.

First of all, the liberals needed to lobby for unconditional US aid to the Republic of India. Then they could see about revising the aid package...
strings.USA_IND.1.a: Sure, Mr. Nehru, it's leverage, but it's damn good leverage!
strings.USA_IND.2.d:
“Damn that bastard Nehru,” muttered Nixon to himself, a scowl resting on his face, “thinks he can play the United States like a goddamn fiddle, not on my watch. I oughta wallop him, teach him a lesson.” The closed doors of the Oval Office served as the only thing keeping the sound of his presidential whinging from becoming public, an outcome that would only further the growing divide between Delhi and DC.

“And those liberal bastards can't get enough when it comes to handing the keys to the country out to those slippery, treacherous people.” He stared down at the Resolute desk, head in hands as his mind went through all the ways he'd learned to deal with Congress when it felt like growing a spine. “I'll, uh, I'll give 'em what they want,” he said, at first quietly and with uncertainty. “Yeah, I'll give them exactly what they want.” He took out his pen, reached for some paper adjacent to him, and began to write.

“They'll never see it coming, they think all I know is crookery and being the man whose name goes along that ungrateful Kennedy.” A smile, or at least an attempt at one, began to grow across his face, progressing slowly from a smirk to a toothy grin. “Streamline aid to India, standardize the shipments, and make sure it's all from this decade and not the last. We'll have 'em by the shorthairs, and the libs'll be my greatest allies in this.” The grin became earnest, although that didn't do much to improve its look.

“Let's see how Nehru likes it when America starts demanding what it's owed.” He pressed the papers upon the desk, assembling them into a pile. “Yes, modern aid for a modern India,” he said, his words dripping with sardonicism.
strings.USA_IND.2.a: And an unhealthy helping of modern imperialism too.
strings.USA_IND.3.d:
The wailing forklifts of the shiny new USAID airport facility definitely did not cure headaches. Aside from that, Nick was rather enjoying the sudden uptick in work to do. Well, maybe not enjoying, but at least it was a nice change of pace from the pile of paperwork per food delivery, most of which until then wasn't even meant to go abroad. Oh, and it was an excuse to re-encounter familiar faces.

“Hiya, Nicky!” The pilot he had flown to Port-au-Prince with a year ago gleamed back at him across a football field of tarmac, his smile overshadowed by a snugly-fitted captain's hat. “Fancy seeing you here. Remember me? The whole mix-up in Haiti?”

“Well, there are only two places for us to see each other anyway,” the aid manager replied. “Wow, it's been a while since Haiti, though. Now we're really going international. Aid to India? Certainly ain't the same trek across the Caribbean, I'll tell you that much.”

“Tell me about it,” the captain sighed. “Heck, I only just heard of Nagpur today, and I'm meant to be flying there in an hour. And don't even get me started on the timetables. I'd never have left the Air Force if I knew this is what I'd be getting into.”

Nick tapped his clipboard with his pencil, reminding himself of all the two-minute turnarounds. “It was... always going to be a step up from Haiti. Kennedy basically founded the whole thing yesterday, and then they decided to leave such a huge brief to us, so we're doing it. We'll get used to the saddle. At least they're not giving us equipment straight out of the war anymore.”

“Heh, I sure hope you're right. But serving a country so far and big will need more than upgrades, I fear. The brass better know what they're doing.”
strings.USA_IND.3.a: It's a long way to New Delhi...
strings.USA_IND.4.d:
Aside from Kennedy's creation, American aid to India was also handled by NGOs - such as private groups, Christian churches, and the American Red Cross. All of them had their different, humanitarian goals, but getting them on the side of the State Department - namely the Red Cross and their resources in particular - would be a major domestic win for Nixon.

There were two ways to go about this. The first was a major increase in US-Indian relations utilizing the American Red Cross. Diplomatic tours of India's most affected areas, relief work, hosting Nehru's boys and the Red Cross leadership at the White House, anything goes. The Indian-American community would be key to ensuring that this renewed effort across the Pacific worked out fine, and it was likely that Nixon would secure their votes for the Republicans in the process too.

The second was to increase support for interventionism across the entire American public, but using the Red Cross's activities in India as an example instead of the military. Getting Indian-American community leaders to coordinate efforts with other communities disaffected by Japanese aggression - such as the Chinese Nationalist exiles and the Korean-Americans - would help raise support for humanitarian intervention overseas, and possibly bring a lot of liberals on board with Nixon.

The final decision lay with Nixon, of course.
strings.USA_IND.4.a: Increase US-Indian relations via the Red Cross.
strings.USA_IND.4.b: Increase support for peaceful intervention among the people.
strings.USA_IND.5.d:
In his grocery store at the corner of 53rd and 24th, Gus Kowalski turns his head away from the conversation he's having with Maggie Lansdale to see where the sound of a bell ringing is coming from outside. It's no fire alarm - just Mr. Singh's kid, Ajay, tall and broad-shouldered and bearded, and ringing a bell with a sandwich board wrapped around his chest - 'Quarters for India', it reads.

The Singhs run the grocery store across from Kowalski's and are a lively, sociable bunch. Gus likes them. He ambles over from the counter to Ajay and shakes his hand. Asks how he's doing, and what cause he's campaigning for.

Ajay passes out pamphlets to the customers in the store. The Republic of India, the homeland of the Singhs, is calling on the Indian diaspora for donations to help the country's brave defense against Japan, against the dictatorship of Azad Hind. India, the largest democracy in South Asia, is facing a civil war started by Japanese meddling - and it needs all the help it can get. No need for big donations - spare change will do. Ajay's not asking for anyone to give up their life savings, eliciting a few laughs from his audience.

Gus's eyes move to a portrait hanging on top of the counter, near the crucifix and the clock. A portrait of a grinning young man in his pinks and greens. Jim had never returned from Mindanao. He'd been found slumped over his machine gun, dead, and with fifteen dead Japanese soldiers in front of him. Died to make men free. And India was doing the same.

Gus walks back to the counter, opens a drawer, and passes Ajay a whole jar of quarters for the collection tin.
strings.USA_IND.6.d:
The Embassy of the United States of America in New Delhi was already a handsome building in itself, that countless American ambassadors considered to rival the Taj Mahal in beauty and grandeur. A 13-acre masterpiece designed by Roger Durell Stone, overlooking a gorgeous tropical water garden with plants, fish, and birds, there was plenty to love about it.

Unfortunately, the increased American efforts in India meant that 13 acres was no longer enough. The embassy was going to need much more space to accommodate all the new offices and agencies operating out of it. Fortunately, the Indian government saw no problem with providing the expansion, on the condition that their domestic construction companies do the job for the Americans. The deal was perfect - the Americans would get their space, and the Indians would get their jobs and money.

So all across fine Chanakyapuri, laborers toiled and machines rolled, engineers surveyed and architects strolled. The expansion of the embassy benefited both parties - the United States now had more influence around not only India but the Italian-controlled Middle East, and India could easily take advantage of that as well to boost their own standing with the non-aligned world.
strings.USA_IND.6.a: Thankfully, the ambassador wasn't too bothered by all the noise.
strings.USA_IND.6_tt: Our ability to conduct CIA operations in the Middle East and India will increase
strings.USA_IND.7.d: Company assets within the Republic of India, including our informants in the ROI's intelligence services, have given us deeply troubling news. The Republic of India and the Azad Hind government are on the brink of pursuing unification negotiations. While the Sphere stands to lose from this, so does the United States - the unified government would definitely remove all foreign influence from within the country, including American interests. Any reintegrated Azad Hind personnel would be able to tear down all American interests built up in India with the stroke of a pen. Langley recommends that all assets in South Asia focus on finding ways to prevent the negotiations from happening. Washington cannot afford to lose the largest democracy in the region.
strings.USA_IND.8.d:
George Wallace had high ambitions when he campaigned for the seat of President and had great expectations for himself once he finally made it to the Oval Office. Sure, Africa was a mess, and aborting Kennedy's little monster wouldn't be simple, but so long as he kept a lid on the bleeding hearts and put on a show of strength to keep the Nazis and bucked-toothed Japanese in check, he was confident he would enjoy a pleasant first year in office. It wasn't so much as a month before he realized that wouldn't happen.

“God damn it. How far can we expect the little bastards to push?” Wallace muttered, tracing his fingers along a map of the Indian-Azad border with one hand while messaging his forehead with the other to stave off a headache. His cabinet stood around the map with him, with grim expressions, with the exceptions of Mills (who looked barely sober) and Byrd (who seemed more concerned about possible Indian refugees coming to the US or its allies), before Brown spoke up.

“Maybe all the way to New Delhi. This isn't the same band of miscreants Bose mangled together in the forties; they've been preparing for this fight since their rump state was founded. And the Japanese are going to be behind them every step.”

“Damn it, alright, fine then.” Wallace took a deep breath before running his fingers through his hair. “Start getting a whip count in the house and senate, and let the Indians know we're coming. We'll wrangle together whatever we got and then some as soon as we get the green light...”
strings.USA_IND.8.a: We're bombing these fascists back to hell.
strings.USA_IND.9.d:
Sometimes, Robert Kennedy wondered how his brother had held it all together. After all those years watching Nixon bumble his way through the White House, from domestic to foreign policy, his brother at least knew what to expect when he finally took over the wayward ship from Nixon. Robert had barely begun to warm up the presidential chair before the world flipped upside down again.

“Alright, let's not mince words here; the global forces of fascism and oppression are on the warpath once again.” His cabinet was assembled around him, and a television screen displayed news reports of ongoing fighting in the sub-continent. “We didn't sit idly when the Germans marched on South Africa; we're not going to let the Sphere ravage India.”

“Getting together support for India isn't going to be easy.” Marine chimed in with a frown. “The universal support for intervention we had for South Africa isn't there anymore; the House and Senate don't want to just bounce from one massive war to another.”

“Then we reach out to the people. They're seeing the carnage already, so we need to make sure they hear our plan to bring it to an end. Convince them to contact their local politicians and get everyone in line. The future of hundreds of millions rests on us, and we will not let them down.” A part of him wondered how Jack would have handled it before putting the thought away.
strings.USA_IND.9.a: The time for doubt has passed.
strings.USA_IND.10.d:
“Good evening, gentlemen,” said Bennett to the cabinet members assembled, “it's uh, not exactly in the brightest of circumstances that we have this meeting, but necessary ones nonetheless. Now Muskie, I'm told you've got some statements prepared.”

“Indeed I do, Mr. President,” he replied. “As of a few hours ago, war has officially broken out between the two Indias. Now, while our relations with the Republic in the west haven't always been perfect, they're no doubt our ally against the Sphere-backed Azad Hind regime in the east.”

“That's, uh, excellent, Muskie. Lovely to hear that. Now, Clifford, I believe you have some remarks as well?”

“Yes, Mr. President. The Republic is currently experiencing a blitz of sorts aimed at the capital: New Delhi. I've got enough connections on the Hill to get some aid through, enough to stall this offensive long enough for our good friends to recuperate.”

“Excellent, excellent,” Bennett said. “I'll make sure you succeed in that; we need to keep them upright until they can hit back.”

“Precisely, sir.”

“Excuse me, Mr. President, but uh, one more thing,” said Bunker.

“Ah, yes, Bunker?”

We're picking up frequent communication between Calcutta and Tokyo, no doubt they'll be sending just as much to them as we will to the Republic. I understand you want a more streamlined OFN, sir, but this is big, and we can't afford to squander this kind of opportunity. In other words, what I'm saying is that escalation isn't off the table.“
strings.USA_IND.11.d:
“I'm being told we've got a situation in the East, gentlemen,” said Johnson, feet atop the Situation Room desk, “been hearing 'bout war on plenty o'tongues.”

“Yes, Mr. President,” replied Rusk, scrambling to affix papers on a display board. “We've been receiving reports of localized skirmishes and rising tensions in the Indian Subcontinent ever since that crazed gunman—not unfortunately, may I add—ended hopes of peace in the region, and it's all finally boiled over.”

“Mm. I assume you'll do your part in sending aid our boys' way. Now, uh, Bob,” he turned his head to face McNamara,“ what're the details on the ground looking like?”

“You see, Mr. President,” he replied, “as of right now, Azad Hind forces are attempting a mad dash toward New Delhi, but if we can help the Republic weather the storm, they'll run out of steam before long. We've just gotta make sure those frontlines stabilize.”

“Sounds good, gentlemen. I still know how to get my way with Congress, so as long as there's a plan, I can whip those spineless bastards into backing it. Dick, got anything to say?”

“Yes Mr. President,” Helms said, “we've, uh, got some contacts in the area, and they're been telling us that Tokyo's doing much the same as us: diplomatic support, intelligence, materiel, they're not intent on letting several hundred million get out of the Sphere's grasp—not when they have millions more to gain.”

“Then we'll just have to outdo them: more guns, more planes, more tanks.”
strings.USA_IND.11.a: “Hell, if I really had my way, I'd just say bomb the bastards.”
strings.USA_IND.12.d:
The Pennsylvanian family sat at the edge of their seats, eyes glued to their television set. But Perry Mason was not playing tonight. Instead, CBS's 24-hour special on India played.

To the grim narration of Walter Cronkite, they watched as the Indian Civil War played out in its bloody spectacle. A beautiful place that most Americans had barely heard of until recently was now in the throes of total war. Villages and cities burned, a horrible tableau of black smoke and orange flame. Crowds of fleeing refugees on foot and bicycle dove into ditches as shells landed around them and planes dropped their bombs - mistaking the sheer size of the crowds for enemy troops. Reporters, unable to keep their composure, wept openly or choked up at the clear signs of starvation on children and infants, the elderly and the women. Desperate signs on scraps of cardboard held up by students, bandaged and bloody - 'HELP US, AMERICA! HELP US!'

The state senator paced in his office, his phone ringing off the hook every minute, every second. The last image had done it nationwide. Quickly, efficiently, at a speed not seen since he was on the campaign trail, he answered the family's desperate call, and moved on to the next.
strings.USA_IND.12.a: “...A crisis not seen since the Japanese swept into Burma in 1942...”
strings.USA_IND_aid_bill_available_tt: A new bill will be available in the Foreign Policy category
strings.USA_IND.13.d:
The bill had passed.

Celebrations erupted across the Pacific as the Republic of India and the diaspora in the OFN rejoiced. The massive escalation of US-led aid shipments from the OFN would be India's salvation, and seriously bolster their war effort. The internationalist factions of American politics were jubilant as well - having been practically vindicated in the immense outpouring of public support and sympathy for the ROI that had followed the bill's passing.

Of course, you can't please everybody, and the usual suspects weren't happy. The isolationists and American Firsters of the media and the public immediately started whining about increased Indian migration to the United States, trying to stir up a panic.

But their hysteria fell on deaf ears as Congress unanimously voted for the stationing of the US 7th Fleet off the Indian coast in a show of anti-fascist force, and additional increases in aid to other OFN allies and OFN-friendly neighbors funding the ROI.

The world's largest democracy would not fight alone, and it had the backing of the Free World behind it.
strings.USA_IND.13.a: As they'd learned many times - one does not simply fight the Japanese alone.
strings.USA_IND.14.d:
The bill had been defeated.

In Washington, the administration rubbed their temples and sighed into their coffee as the Republic of India politely expressed their dismay, and the diaspora in the OFN held peaceful protests in disappointment. At several protests in the United States, Indian-Americans were confronted by isolationist counter-protesters who were whipping a worrying amount of the American public into an anti-immigration frenzy yet again. The internationalist factions of American politics wrote bitterly about their defeat.

Public sympathy for the ROI was still high, though, and the administration needed to get creative with aid. One idea was to use any loose funds over from the aid programs to feed into India, and to grab any aid from other countries who weren't an urgent priority, such as Iceland, Haiti, and Belize. And a campaign throughout the OFN to support the ROI, to aid them when the US, unfortunately, couldn't, would do much to help the ROI out at the cost of American prestige.
strings.USA_IND.14.a: Uncle Sam had fumbled India and was kicking himself for it.
strings.USA_IND.15.d:
New problems require new solutions, and the India aid plan was certainly a novel conundrum. A country so large with needs so great and a position so disconnected could not rely on one country, or organization, to bear the costs and thus motivation. Therefore, it made sense to rely on multiple.

The OFN-OAS aid coalition, while relying on American logistical muscle to distribute, could channel donations from many contributors across the membership of those organizations, and thus a hefty pool of potential resources to work on when trouble came for the Indian subcontinent.

But how “potential” these resources truly are also spells trouble: one could hardly guarantee an indifferent senator or head of state would not strike it down. Was it worth going through the trouble of petitioning the North and South American states to then be left alone by the OFN, or vice versa? Moreover, was it worth the additional backlash and funding when there were so many other things to protest federal funding for?

In the end, India's money went through the White House, and its owner had to make the final call. When it came to the coalition plan...
strings.USA_IND.16.d:
As the east of the country boiled in a bloodbath, as soldiers came home bruised and battered to the cities, they saw the war they fought retold for a different audience, in a different light. Images of sinister men grinning in topis, marching in, destroying, violating what was meant to be Hindu, Indian land.

They heard the story played out again and again of Bengali usurpers, Muslims desecrating the holy sites in Varanasi and Ayodhya. Mobile cinemas and leaflets toured the country from Puducherry to the Punjab, telegraphing the tale to the masses of Muslim invaders committing unspeakable acts to non-Muslim prisoners of war, reversing all the efforts toward freedom of the past twenty years.

It hardened the wills of some, struck fear into the hearts of many, emboldened the angry to riot and the attacked to flee. It no longer mattered whether true or untrue, whether the swirling stories were rumors in the barracks or portents of a real threat to come. The CIA's operation of sectarian subterfuge staked a new front in the war, right in the middle of Indian society.
strings.USA_IND.17.d:
Following its total victory over Azad Hind with American aid, the Republic of India had become an official OFN partner, allowing it to preserve its non-alignment while strengthening ties with the United States.

While certain hawks grumbled about India's refusal to bind itself to the United States, the mood in Washington was jubilant, and the rest of the OFN was rejoicing. By securing the largest democracy in South Asia, Japan had been dealt a hammer blow by the OFN as it had effectively lost any potential dominance over the Indian subcontinent. Thanks to them aiding the ROI in its hour of need, the OFN now had a reliable base of operations in continental Asia, opening new opportunities to strike the Sphere in their own backyard!

The Indian-American diaspora led the celebrations across the United States, and in solidarity with their people back in the ROI. The Free World had gained a new member - one that many were betting would become the world's largest democracy, and a powerful juggernaut against Japanese fascism.
strings.USA_IND.18.d:
As President {usa_getleader} walked through the promenade and up the stairs leading to Rashtrapati Bhavan—the latest visitor to change history behind its towering columns—he felt a jolt pass through his body, as if suddenly aware of the gravity of these fleeting moments. Before him,. {ind_getleader} looked ahead, offering an extended hand.

Just years prior, the relationship between the two democracies had been strained and volatile, fraught with points of contention throughout. But now, with the wise custodianship of Swatantra in Delhi and the benevolent humanitarianism of DC—or so the briefings read—that past was behind them both. He clasped {ind_getleader}'s hand, careful to moderate his firmness. It would not be an opportune moment for a slight.

Looking to his right, the sheer scale of the crowd awed him. The vigilant security details, the imposing palatial complex, the treaty to change the world, they all faded into the background, however briefly. He looked back, his mind finally acknowledging that that stuffy plane ride had been more than worth it. Up. Down. Up. Down. They shook a few times more, then turned to face the crowd—and the podium.

Taking another look at the cityscape, he saw a few buildings still bearing the scars of war. Next to them, freshly constructed ones provided effective contrast. The two presidents each grabbed pens from their respective sides of the wooden stand, flanking the paper lying upon it. Twin flourishes of the wrist carved paths of ink upon the colorless treaty, upon the unimposing treaty, not befitting the change it had wrought. The people, however, cheered all the same as the two dancers took the stage exits. He could almost hear them crying out for an encore.
strings.USA_IND.19.t: To the Victor's Allies Go the Spoils
strings.USA_IND.19.d:
One thing Barry Astor was all-too familiar with was that the commotion of urban life was a routine and deafening force. But as the landing gear of his private jet extended down, settling it upon the hastily repaired tarmac, it became clear that even it could be disturbed. And as Astor, enterprising investor, or so said his résumé, descended from the plane's airstair and gazed upon the rubble that once made up Calcutta, there was only one thing on his mind: profit.

His guide quickly approached him, taking him off to the side and away from the war's aftermath. Not a good look for discerning customers, after all. They entered an open-top jeep, the guide's foot on the gas accelerating them toward fields of green leaves sprouting from rich, black soil. They disembarked, feet on the ground once more in order to more closely inspect the farm—no, the venture before them. The better part of one-hundred laborers extracted leaves—no, profit from the tea crops before them. This scene repeated itself tens of times across the landscape, taking up acres in what the guide had called a “noble pursuit to make use of nature's bounty.”

The visuals were, on their own, enough to convince Astor to buy. He'd been scouting out locations for A&P for a little while now, searching for the next addition to their roster of produce. Some of the workers appeared emaciated, but he paid no heed. So too, did he pay no heed to the sound of gunshots in the urban jungle turned wasteland behind him. They did not warrant it. What did, however, was the green being collected before him and the different green to be collected after.

“Thank you Swatantra,” he muttered to himself, because after this, the supermarkets would have a little more variety, and a lot more profit.
strings.USA_IND.19.a: And the laborers would see none of it.
strings.USA_IND.20.d:
Across the breadth of the Indian subcontinent, a collective sigh of relief is released into the air, mingling with the air currents circulating throughout. From there, it does not take long for news to travel. From east to west, Sphere to OFN, Eurus to Zephyrus, there is one word on the minds of all with even the most fleeting knowledge of global affairs: Peace.

Across the breadth of the United States, from sea to shining sea, a collective spark of hope is lit, however brief and small, as stories of negotiation triumphing over bloodshed conjure images of an end to the world's sorrows. But while it may leave within the week, for the next day remains ahead, it carries the one word capable of, even for a moment, and even without much consequence, bringing about within the minds of millions an outlook of optimism: Peace.

Across the breadth of the whole of D.C. and the many buildings therein, whether the Capitol or an unassuming office, a collective feeling of frustration takes hold of the powerbrokers, the legislators, the executors; it almost possesses them, yet such a statement would belie the fact that such an infuriated disposition is one that has come from within. Delhi and Calcutta becoming one without need for a single shot fired may have been the action, but the reaction is the fault of those reacting alone, those reacting with such vitriol in the face of an ordinarily joyous occasion: Peace.

Across the nearly eleven meter wide breadth of the Oval Office, among the commander-in-chief, the head of the executive branch, the leader of the free world, the man behind the Resolute desk and his cabinet, a collective indignatory rage receives an invitation from the minds of those assembled and takes its entry eagerly, for there is a concept that, in the minds of a few, is worth clouding one's judgment in the face of: Peace.
strings.USA_IND.20.a: And they would make a desert of it yet.
strings.USA_IND.21.d:
The sound of the Speaker's gavel hitting the sound block reverberated throughout the House, putting discussions on hold as it echoed from wall to wall. Eight-hundred-sixty-eight eyes looked at two.

Like an automaton, in a routine many-times-rehearsed, the speaker began to read out the results of bills, each awaiting a chance at acthood. The senses of most lost interest rapidly, with most bills utterly inconsequential, with their results a foregone conclusion. But as the counting of yeas and nays continued, a sense of apprehension began to fill the room. With each meaningless formality spoken aloud, a new chance—each greater than the last—at the subject of this growing interest appearing was born, before promptly giving way. Yet just three bills away from the final one of the session, it appeared.

“A bill for the granting of aid to the Republic of India in the interest of the national security of the United States of America,” said the speaker, and in spite of its unwieldy title—one that would certainly be made more literarily photogenic as the headlines hit—the thought of the next few words gave the chamber a newfound sense of focus.

“The voting record states,” he dryly continued, yet the tone did little to dampen the enthusiasm of the body, “Three-hundred-seventy-six for Yea, fifty-seven for Nay, and two Present.”

Three-hundred-seventy-six rejoiced, fifty-seven were silent, and two were silent. The sound of the gavel rang throughout the building yet again, although it took an additional slam to quiet the room down. Even still, news of aid, humanitarian and otherwise, kept the yea voters smiling, and even those merely present couldn't help but share a bit of the joy. A letter would be drafted to {usa_getleader} shortly, and the OFN's presence on the global stage would receive the reinforcements it desired, that much, at the very least, was for certain.
strings.USA_IND.21.a: That is, so long as the Senate was just as willing.
strings.USA_IND_aid_bill_senate_tt: The bill has passed the House - but the Senate may be more resistant.
strings.USA_IND.22.d:
The crunching of boots on gravel filled the cramped, hot Lahore consulate with yet more stress. A staffer looked out of a window, spotting militiamen investigating local buildings for any signs of resistance lying in wait. A sharp rap on the door caused him to recoil from the glass in shock, and a glance at his coworkers confirmed his position as closest to the door, and therefore the one with responsibility for opening it. Desperate times call for desperate unspoken agreements, he supposed.

“This is the Consulate General of the United States in Lahore, please state your business,” he said in almost fluent Punjabi. The man, however, responded in Pashto. “Punjabi?” he asked. The man then stepped aside, and another took his place.

“This city is the territory of the Republ—er, Dominion of Pakistan,” the other man said, the language barrier now removed. “State your business.”

“This is, as has been stated in the past, a diplomatic mission on behalf of the United States.” Beads of sweat, no longer caused entirely by the sweltering heat, began their descent from the staffer's face. He hoped they did not betray fear.

“And to what nation is this diplomatic mission currently being conducted with?” he said, prompting the lump in the staffer's throat to grow larger and demanding the response he would do anything not to give.

“To the Republic of India,” he said with a sigh, “this mission is currently being conducted with the Republic of India, and we request that in light of extenuating circumstances the matter not be discussed further.”

“Interesting. Do inform us of any updates on these 'extenuating circumstances' should they arise. We are quite interested, after all.
strings.USA_IND.22.a: “And we eagerly await our next visit.”
strings.USA_IND.23.d:
The consul-general could have killed that kid. It was too early to even look at them, let alone talk; they were protected by the stars and stripes and twenty armed men underneath it; he was not authorised to say a word to anyone outside the consulate now that ibn Qasim turned Lahore into enemy territory. He'd have to make do with a censure and a poor performance review if they both made it out alive. Slim chance; Pakistani police were camped somewhere east, riot cops lined the streets outside, and they'd cut the regional phone lines so he couldn't get a clear message out to Delhi.

A friendly cop tipped off the consul-general to the raid minutes before it hit, enough time for him to run up and down, telling everyone to burn and shred. Seven minutes passed, cables curling up in heat, letters cut and scattered. In his third-floor office, he packed two suitcases: one personal, one professional. Anything sensitive he couldn't take with him was consigned to his own fire. When those seven minutes were up, the cops outside moved into position. Main team knocked down the gate and the front door with a battering ram; another team cut in through the side. Beneath him, the consul-general heard panic, furniture thrown out of place, multilingual shouting and cursing.

Cops were still a few minutes away from the first floor. The consul-general panicked, ran downstairs to the second-floor. There was an office with a privacy hedge covering its window. He entered, locked the door and cracked the window open. His baseball days and the trim figure they required were long gone, but he could still squeeze through. He threw the briefcases through, heard them clatter a long way below, but as he stuck his upper body through the window he could reach out, grab the hedges and maybe climb them-

The door flung open with a kick. The consul-general panicked, tried to scramble out, but the Pakistani cops hauled him out by his ankles.
strings.USA_IND.23.a: He went with them, screaming nothing they cared to understand.
strings.USA_IND_rescue_staffers_tt: A new CIA operation to rescue our staffers is available
strings.USA_IND.24.d:
As the sounds of gunfire and shelling across the subcontinent faded, it was a quiet morning in Lahore when the American staffers shuffled out again from the Pakistani prison, blindfolded, weak, and lips parched with thirst. They stood stock-still as their guards undid their blindfolds. This time, it was not another Pakistani Army delegation that stood before them, but American members of the International Red Cross flanked by United States Marines. A few words in English were exchanged between the Pakistani officer and the American ambassador to Pakistan, before the Pakistanis turned on their heels and headed back inside.

Forgetting their thirst and their exhaustion, the staffers cheered and wept with joy when they realized what was happening. The war was over, the crisis was over. They were going home.

While the hostages flew back to Washington D.C. as the United States celebrated the end of the crisis, and Welcome Home signs were prepared in various American households, the President's staffers were jubilant as well. Although it was an embarrassment that the military couldn't rescue the staffers themselves, the President's popularity had gotten a minor boost in ratings for their determined handling of the crisis, and their unyielding approach to pro-German Pakistan.
strings.USA_IND.24.a: Uncle Sam rejoices as his sons and daughters come home.
strings.USA_IND.25.d:
Despite their resounding military victory over Azad Hind, there is increasing feeling within the Republic of India that one enemy has been replaced with another. The new nation of Pakistan sees India as an existential threat, and has repeatedly refused to withdraw any of their mutual territorial claims. Together with Pakistan's oligarchic authoritarianism and their 'fascistic' territorial claims, the ROI is positioning itself for another struggle between democracy and dictatorship in a future confrontation between India and Pakistan.

Chief to this future confrontation is the 776-kilometer (482 mile) military control line running between the disputed territory of Kashmir. Popularly known as the 'Line of Control', the LOC divides Kashmir between Pakistani and Indian-controlled territories. It is not recognized as a legal international boundary by the OFN or the Einheitspakt, but across the LOC, the Indian and Pakistani armies stare each other down daily, and running battles between Pakistani-backed paramilitaries and Indian troops occur throughout Kashmir.

Tensions continue to gradually increase across the subcontinent; border exercises, artillery duels, airspace violations, shouting matches between officers, and most concerning of all, a rapidly expanding shadow war between the Indian intelligence services and Pakistan's formidable security agencies. Supposedly the object of their intense activity is to prevent the rival government from developing nuclear weapons. Neither Washington or Germania have made statements on this matter.
strings.USA_IND.25.a: One threat has been replaced with another.
strings.USA_IND.26.t: The End of the Pakistan Experiment
strings.USA_IND.26.d:
The Pakistan Movement's forces broke upon Punjab - the so-called “martial race” defeated, and their strongholds in the North-West Frontier occupied, and coming with that, the end of German influence in the Indian subcontinent. Already, its military officers, fundamentalist fanatics, and its oligarchical, callous aristocracy are fleeing like rats in the dark of night, scrambling away with their gold and their prayers to Germany or Iran. Any pitiful insurgency resulting from this will be crushed, as the government in exile set up by them impotently rants on about the Americo-Indian hydra.

Reintegration is not without its challenges, but the government is more than prepared to uproot the Pakistan experiment and its failures. Pakistan and their German backers have left scars and damage, but it's not unfixable, and already grassroots efforts are on the ground doing what they can to help those trampled underfoot by the Pakistani rebels.

And moreover, the idea of India being partitioned is over - the subcontinent is united in spirit although perhaps not in fact, never to be divided again by imperialist power plays - be it the British Empire or the Third Reich.
strings.USA_IND.27.d:
The Republic of India, the star of the OFN in South Asia, has been deposed. America has lost its foothold in the subcontinent, the world's largest democracy seemingly vanished in a flash. There is a silver lining, if an uncomfortable choice - Pakistan has broken off from India.

While claiming to uphold the principles of Islamic democracy and a safe haven for oppressed Muslim minorities in India, the Islamic Republic of Pakistan is an oligarchic state run by a mix of powerful aristocrats, pocketed politicians, and ambitious military officers. Pakistan is also aligned with Germany and Europe, an outpost of German influence in South Asia, and on the doorstep of the Sphere to boot.

In normal times, Pakistan would be considered a potential enemy of the Free World. But these are extraordinary times, and they call for extraordinary measures. For all its trumpeting of its ties with Germany, Pakistan's elite will be just as happy with dollars as they are Reichsmarks, and may be open to American involvement. This could range from investment, to backchannel military cooperation, to even covert operations.
strings.USA_IND.27.a: Lahore reaches out to Washington, and waits for a handshake.
strings.USA_IND.28.d:
The Indian War has drawn to a close as the pro-Japanese government of Azad Hind have defeated both India and Pakistan in what many are calling one of the biggest upsets for the OFN in recent years. The congratulations ring from Tokyo as one of their most powerful assets in the region has proved its military might, while Washington and Berlin slink away in shame. The United States has been hit particularly hard, having invested heavily into shoring up India as a major line of defense against Japan.

With India's defeat, the President of the United States and their party have suffered a major bump in polling as America takes a huge slide towards isolationism again - an embarrassing defeat for Washington, and an ominous sign of a grim future to many in the OFN, and to America's anti-fascist allies.
strings.USA_IND.29.d:
Of all the forms of American involvement in stabilizing Pakistan, the cooperation between the CIA and Pakistani intelligence may prove the most fruitful to American interests. The civilian government, while pro-German, is amenable to American involvement in exchange for American money, and the local intelligence community is eager to learn from the best, and the CIA are just that.

With another show of generous support from Washington, the CIA has established and embedded itself firmly in Lahore, beginning to build an intelligence network throughout Pakistan and into Free India. While CIA agents report that the Pakistani FIA is in no way known for its competence or for its incorruptibility, they have proven eager to assist in the destabilisation of Azad Hind. Ironically, one of the main methods being used are attempts to cast Azad Hind as a Muslim-dominated nation, to inflame the Hindu majority into igniting communal violence.

Internally speaking, Pakistani intelligence has a laser focus solely on trade unionists and advocates of land reform, who are eagerly branded and executed as “communists”. The CIA are, of course, not averse to this, and have begun to use American connections to Pakistani academics to collect lists of possibly dangerous socialist figures there.

Although neither would admit it, the Ausland-SD and the CIA now find themselves joining hands, to stabilise the Pakistani government, and shatter India's unity.
strings.USA_IND.29.a: Two eagles fly together, to set the Ganges ablaze once more.
strings.USA_IND.231.d:
An operation to rescue American hostages from the government's besieged consulate in Lahore, currently occupied by terrorists from the Pakistani Movement, has ended in disaster. It is believed that the Marine team put in place for the operation was discovered by security forces after a police officer noticed an illegally parked vehicle outside the consulate, tipping him off to the ongoing infiltration inside.

To avoid provoking an international incident, the Marines have been returned home, but not the captured staffers. President {usa_getleader} has refused to respond to questions from our reporters, but private sources from inside his party have signaled their fury at how he has handled this operation, with many calling it one of the greatest ever mishaps in American foreign policy history.
strings.USA_IND.231.a: I don't want to hear another word about this...
strings.USA_INS.1.desc:
Chef Henry Haller prepared a set of club sandwiches to go out. Deli fare wasn't his specialty, but there was a major meeting going on upstairs on short notice, and he didn't really have time to prepare a more sumptuous meal. “Just a minute!” he called out in his well-known Swiss accent to the butler. “We are still getting the side salad ready.” He took a breath. “What is even going on in the Oval Office?”

“Indonesia, Henry,” said butler Eugene Allen. “Defense, State, CIA, they're all down there.”

“That thing with the pilot and the Australian boat?” Allen nodded. “So we've finally had enough of them, haven't we?”

“Maybe, but it's just another disaster to throw onto the pile. Africa is a mess, we're stuck there, and now we have another war on the horizon in a far off place. I don't see getting into it being very popular.”

“So, if that is the situation, then I guess we stay out of it.” Haller took a completed bowl of salad and started dishing out the portions. “There are too many wars, we cannot win all of them, and we cannot get into all of them either.”

“That's what the President is concerned about, but the secretaries are telling him otherwise.” Allen loaded the plates onto his tray. “I was in there, they were saying the Austrailians for one thing - they aren't going to be happy with a no. They want to see that Sukarno fella out about as much as we wanted to see Hüttig dead. And they are saying the United States simply can't leave it all up to them, or the Japanese take the entire region.”

Haller was silent as he finished dishing out the last portions. “All right Allen, I think you should tell me what the President decides.”
strings.USA_INS.2.desc:
The cheers of happy White House staff members could be heard from below, as Chef Haller prepared the celebratory meal. Nasi goreng with fried egg, prawn crackers, and pickles. Ikan bakar grilled fish. Sayur asem vegetable soup. Steamed rice in banana leaf. Not exactly the typical fare he imagined himself would be cooking in the United States, and certainly it had a few recipes he had never heard of before the war began. But this preparation would not go to waste. This was the celebration, all those long nights, stresses, and setbacks, all of that had come to an end.

“That's another one Henry!” Allen shouted as he came in. “We beat the Japanese, Sukarno, all those goons! I haven't seen this place so happy since Eisenhower was re-elected.”

“And I suppose the city is excited as well?”

“I called Helene and everyone on the block is excited. Most of them know someone in the service, and they're coming back. They can argue if it was right or wrong, but we won and it's over.”

“Perhaps,” Haller said as he tasted the Sayur asem. “But they say Hatta may stay in the Sphere at the end of all this. Is it really true? Was it all worth it?”

“Hatta may enter the Sphere, but it will be on his terms, not Tokyo's. And there are quite a few people behind him who know who got them there.” He picked up the tray. “The diner can decide what he wants, but the kitchen cooks it how the chef likes it.”

“Quite right, Mister Allen,” Haller smiled.
strings.USA_INS.2.a: Serve with a side of Sambal.
strings.USA_INS.3.desc:
There had been days when Eugene Allen hated this job. The dissonance of watching men of his skin color fight and die for their rights when he was tasked with pretending everything was normal to the elite of the United States. When Kennedy died, he took on the reception for the funeral. And today was going to be one of those days, as he looked at the somber faces of soldiers, diplomats, Australian dignitaries, and assorted staff of the White House as they looked at the TV screen.

It was CBS News. Footage showing the Huey helicopters departing the Indonesian archipelago, pulling out the last OFN troops as the world closed in. Shots of government tanks rolling into the cities once held by the Free Indonesians. Crowds of refugees, people who once had been loyal to the cause begging to get the hell out at the airfield, clutching at the wheels of aircraft and crowding aboard the C-130s. And here they were, on the other side of the world, watching it all fall apart as Allen served light alcoholic drinks from his tray.

Eugene hated this surreal fantasy world, but when he got home, he knew it would be worse. He knew the people on his block had sons abroad in the service. Some were on those last flights out. Some of those would never leave, or were already in Arlington. They were disgusted with it all, and they would translate that disgust to him. One of the good ones, an Uncle Tom, a house negro, someone far away from this world of pain they were forced to live in.

The free world had failed, its blood, bombs, and bonds coming to naught. The people in this room had failed to defeat the Sphere at a tremendous cost. And Eugene had to worry about looking his son in the eyes and saying - yes, this was the greatest country on earth - and having nothing sincere to back it up.
strings.USA_INS.4.desc:
In the White House, a meeting room was dead silent save for the voice of the Secretary of State. Quietly listening around a table were the President, his cabinet, and the Australian ambassador. News of the Indonesian War's conclusion had finally reached Washington, and now everyone anticipated what their next move would be.

“In short, Free Indonesia has won.” The Secretary of State's remarks were met by a round of cheering at the news. However, the man speaking did not share their excitement. As the noise died down, he continued reading. “However, the government is led by Zulkifli Lubis, not Hatta. Given his cooperation with Suharto, it's unclear how much he can be trusted.”

Hearing the last piece quickly sunk everyone's mood. Suddenly their investment had seemed a lot more questionable, especially considering some pro-Japanese elements might still be lurking in the background with the Suharto. No one wanted to address the room.

Except for the Australian ambassador, who ended up breaking the silence.

“Well, it might not be our preferred guy, but at least we've given Tokyo a black eye. That's at least something we can give to the public, even if it won't assuage the families of the dead. I'm satisfied, gentlemen.”

As the ambassador left, the President looked to his Secretary of State over the whole affair. Both men possessed confused expressions, but neither could say the ambassador was wrong. As the President dismissed the meeting, he began to think about what had been the greater victory for them in the conflict, Indonesia - or Australia.
strings.USA_INS.5.desc:
It was funny, Chef Haller thought. He used to take care in sourcing his ingredients when he was working at the hotels. Granted, he had to accept some level of restriction when he started work in the White House. Security concerns prevented him from using the same supplier or grocer too many times, but he still had a general list of places he liked. But in the cafeteria, they only had one type of coffee, and he didn't know where it came from. He looked into the cup, and wondered. Guatemala? Mexico? Brazil? Or maybe -

“Do you think we will be getting Javanese coffee, Mister Allen?” he thought aloud, alluding to the day's news.

Eugene Allen shrugged. “Perhaps the Indonesians will sell us some now that they won,” he said. “But for some reason... a lot of people aren't happy about it here.”

“How so?” asked Chef Haller.

“They seem to think they missed an opportunity,” Edward explained. “If the President went all in, they could have kicked the door wide open and defeated the Japanese for a massive political boost. Not to mention have a lot more of the Indonesians be dependent on the United States for getting them there.”

Haller thought it over, taking a bite of the donut. “Mister Allen,” he said, “when I was a younger man, I was in the Swiss Army after being called up for war. Every time I went to the theatres, I saw Warsaw, Rotterdam, London, Moscow, all the great cities of Europe go up in flames, the Nazis smashing through any resistance, and I was worried we - little Switzerland - would be next. And I feared I would die at a young age, never to accomplish my dreams. But fortunately, the war never came, and I got to grow up and be in one of the greatest jobs on earth. Do you understand me?”

Eugene nodded. “I think I do. We won a war we didn't fight.”
strings.USA_INS.6.desc:
The tension in the White House was so thick you could... no, thought Chef Haller as he sliced up the onions for the President's chili. Too obvious, too cliche, too, well, light for this miserable day.

From when he read the news, he knew this was going to be a terrible day. Everyone knew the OFN had failed in the far east, and everyone was angry about it. Some believed the Indonesians had failed, others that the Australians had not finished the job through. But still others had their own ideas. They were the ones who urged US intervention, that they could have won the conflict if the US bothered to get involved.

Now, the conflict was lost, and maybe everyone was right about how it failed. Or perhaps none of them were. But the ones who argued the President had failed were the loudest. If they had listened to them, Indonesia might be free, the Japanese would be the ones kicked off the islands, and Tokyo would be sweating it out and not them. They had their own group in the White House, cutting across a wide swath of the people who came and went today, and certainly everyone was ready to burst.

Eugene Allen entered in his butler's uniform, not saying a word, heading straight for the liquor cabinet. He looked Haller right in the face, an expression of mutual understanding. He got out the ice and glasses, then paused, deep in thought. Eugene asked “you want to know what I think?”

“What do you think, Mister Allen?”

“If we had lost... and we had our sons and fathers over there...”

Allen shook his head and walked off, leaving Haller in the kitchen with the onions.
strings.USA_INS.6.a: It wasn't stirred constantly on the boiler.
strings.USA_INS.7.desc:
There they were, the President, his cabinet, and the Australians, all shuffling silently into the room. The cold reality of the situation made them all awake, all very sober to process what happened.

“SUHARTO WINS.” Two simple black words on the morning's newspaper spelt out the new reality. They spent a lot of time, both in that meeting and others, reflecting on what went wrong and how they lost so much. It was true that in the course of that long, drawn-out war - a war that cost many American lives and much more in the lives of the Indonesians themselves - there were moments when it seemed that the tide was turning, that they really could win.

Wasn't it because of this hope that they sent so many of their sons to fight in the jungles? Was their confidence so misplaced? What, then, could they say to the grieving families welcoming the body bags back home? Was it all worthless?

Well, they could tell them the truth. That Suharto was never interested in working with America even before the war. That, with all threats to his power eliminated, Suharto would take Indonesia in his own direction, which would be as far away from the OFN as possible. That, ultimately, Tokyo had won the fight and that America's boys died for nothing.

Of course, they couldn't tell them that. They'd throw out the same banal platitudes they always did and hoped they would help. But no cliche could erase what everyone - both within the room and without - knew:
strings.USA_INS.8.desc:
“Wait: I want to make sure I understand this. So after Lubis and Suharto basically coup the Indonesian government and kick out Sukarno - after everything that's already happened in the last few years - they then lose to, of all people, the opposition?” President {usa_getleader} interrupted the briefing by the Secretary of State, looking just as confused as the Cabinet. Describing the mood in the Situation Room as confused would probably be underselling the sheer bewilderment present on everyone's faces.

The Secretary of State cleared his throat. “Yes. It appears so. This shouldn't have been possible, but then again, nobody expected Lubis and Suharto to go for that power grab either.'

'To summarize, the situation on the ground is rapidly spiraling out of control,' he continued. 'We doubt that the new government can control the chaos any better than the previous ones. Even if we'd like to help, they haven't reached out to us at all. I don't think they're interested.”

The President examined the myriad documents on the table. They didn't need to be read in detail: the pictures of a broken Djakarta told the story well enough. After letting out a sigh, they spoke, making their frustration obvious.

“Let's take a step back here. Do you know what this means? This was the chink in the Sphere's armor. This was meant to be our beachhead into the Sphere! At least Tokyo doesn't have it: that would be worse.”
strings.USA_INS.8.a: “But I doubt we'll ever get an opportunity like this again.”
strings.USA_INS.9.desc:
The State Department has been filled with chaos as the Indonesian Civil War takes a new, unexpected turn. Confused and angry diplomats have been pacing around their offices, making calls to contacts in Indonesia that never get returned. Even the CIA is unsure of what to make of things, as contacts on the ground report a similar lack of information. To both the President and the public, the image of events has been quite maddening.

Our Australian allies are similarly miffed at the whole affair, seeing one of the primary interests in the region seemingly go up in flames despite our investment. They stand by us and the President in sheer frustration over recent events.

Hatta has appeared to have lost any form of control over the Free Indonesia government, as has Sukarno over the Indonesian government. Under Zulkifli Lubis and Suharto, the context of the war has been completely upended, and a regime is now in place in Djakarta far from what we wanted when we originally began sending men and materiel to Indonesia.

At the very least, Lubis - President Lubis - seems to be the one more in control between the two, and he does possess some sympathies to the OFN from all the aid allotted to him. However, it comes as little relief to the State Department, the President, the troops returning home, and the people who now demand answers on the meaning of the Indonesian conflict after so many twists.
strings.USA_INS.10.desc:
The State Department has been filled with chaos as the Indonesian Civil War takes a new, unexpected turn. Confused and angry diplomats have been pacing around their offices, making calls to contacts in Indonesia that never get returned. Even the CIA is unsure of what to make of things, as contacts on the ground report a similar lack of information. To both the President and the public, the image of events has been quite maddening.

Our Australian allies are similarly miffed at the whole affair, seeing one of the primary interests in the region seemingly go up in flames despite our investment. They stand by us and the President in sheer frustration over recent events.

Hatta has appeared to have lost any form of control over the Free Indonesia government, as has Sukarno over the Indonesian government. Under Suharto and Zulkifli Lubis, the context of the war has been completely upended, and a regime is now in place in Djakarta far from what we wanted when we originally began sending men and materiel.

Even worse, Suharto - now President Suharto - appears to have absorbed what remains of the Free Indonesian government, all thanks to Lubis stabbing us in the back. To the dismay of our advisors, Suharto is likely to cozy up again back to Japan. There is nothing else to say other than that we have been bamboozled. All that is left is for the President to turn back to the nation, and try to explain our previous actions in a way that mollifies the anger of the electorate.
strings.USA_INS.11.desc:
An uncomfortable silence filled the Situation Room as the final speaker wrapped up their presentation. Someone coughed, then quickly suppressed it, sensing the gravity of the situation. All eyes were on the President, who took a few moments to process everything that was happening.

At the beginning of the war the costs seemed to be manageable. They were tough to bear, of course, but they were still acceptable, even noble - as long as they didn't increase. But month by month the reports grew longer and longer, culminating in last month's reports, which showed such a high jump in casualties and lost equipment that it startled the usually nonplussed National Security Council.

This month's reports, which they looked forward to, were supposed to reverse this trend. Instead, the trend only accelerated. President {usa_getleader} picked up one of the reports. It was clear that fighting had now spread across the entire country, and increasingly their boys had to fill in gaps in Hatta's Free Indonesian Army - with the resulting casualties.

A stray idea weaseled its way into President {usa_getleader}'s mind. What if the US left the war, just cut their losses and ran? That thought was immediately rubbished. Even if you ignored the enormous stakes, America had paid far too high a cost to leave with nothing.

So they would continue, then: more of their boys will die in Indonesian jungles. America will have to endure. All eyes were on the President, all in anxious anticipation of what the decision would be. The words that were spoken would leave no doubt of their resolve.
strings.USA_INS.11.a: “We must win this war. There's no turning back.”
strings.USA_INS.12.desc:
“With all due respect, Ambassador Fukuda, the evidence we have is utterly indisputable,” the President said. “America expects, at minimum, a formal apology, substantial compensation for our losses, and a total withdrawal of all Japanese troops from Indonesia.”

The Japanese ambassador was indignant. “What lies! We are innocent. Us, apologizing to you? Pah: it should be the reverse! You, accusing us of killing your men, when it is clear as day that you are murdering our soldiers. But forget it. This is a waste of time.” Before the President could respond, the ambassador got up to leave, slamming the door as he went out.

After the ambassador slammed the door shut President {leader_name} let out a breath he didn't even know he was holding. This meeting was much more tense than anything else he'd had in a while, but there were good reasons to be worried.

By now even the general public was aware that both America and Japan had soldiers in Indonesia. Most were blissfully unaware of the deeper implications. With nary a soul noticing, what was once unthinkable had become a reality. American and Japanese soldiers were shooting each other, killing each other.

Of course they couldn't say that out loud. Both the President and the ambassador realized what would happen if they did: it'd be a race to the top of the escalation ladder where the only prize was nuclear annihilation. Even as their armies were slaughtering each other with all the destructive force that only modern war could bring, both sides had to pretend it wasn't actually a war.

There they were, America and Japan, locked in this uncomfortable pas de deux:
strings.USA_INS.12.a: It was right to worry about how long this facade could last.
strings.USA_INS.100.desc:
CLASSIFICATION: TOP SECRET

CENTRAL INTELLIGENCE AGENCY | DIRECTORATE OF INTELLIGENCE
Subject: Permesta & North Sulawesi

The growing tide of dissent against the Sukarno regime has continued to nurture special opportunities for us to undermine the Tokyo-backed government in Djakarta. One such venue is the Universal Struggle Charter movement (aka Permesta), whose leaders seek to oppose and fight against the constricting economic policies damaging their local business developments. Furthermore, it is noted that a popular dissatisfaction against the regime has swept the province of North Sulawesi, granting us the boon of striking two birds with one stone.

If the operation, codenamed “Fire Sale”, is greenlit, it will proceed as two-fold. Firstly, we will provide the local Permesta group with a supply of weapons and equipment, alongside a small unit of military instructors to train the rebels in using them, should civil war break out. Secondly, we will utilize the North Sulawesi region as a logistics hub to provide our soldiers in the USFIP in Mindanao with much-needed support in their ongoing struggle against the Philippine Garrison.

At your word, Mr. President, we will begin the operation immediately.
strings.USA_INS.100.a: Give those boys their guns and ammo.
strings.USA_INS.101.desc:
CLASSIFICATION: TOP SECRET

CENTRAL INTELLIGENCE AGENCY | DIRECTORATE OF INTELLIGENCE
Subject: The Copra Colonels

Our agents in the field have successfully made contact with elements of the Indonesian Army in Sumatra affiliated with the “Copra Colonels”: a rival faction against the dominant PETA clique of generals dictating military policy from Java (see Memorandum - Factionalism within the Indonesian Armed Forces). After managing to secure trust with the Copra Colonels, we were able to make contact directly with the group's leadership themselves, among them a Colonel Ahmad Husein.

Colonel Husein had expressed a growing resentment among his men due to the lackluster resources he had been provided by the government to perform his duties, and had begun to seek out funding to accomplish that task. After discussing the possibility of receiving American capital among other things to invest in his forces, the Colonel has demonstrated a willingness to “act” upon his dissatisfaction against Djakarta, as long as we provide better benefits to persuade him.

Such an exploit could prove invaluable in undermining the unity of the Indonesian Army and weaken the regime's hold upon the region. At your behest, Mr. President, we could begin the process of further negotiation.
strings.USA_INS.102.desc:
CLASSIFICATION: TOP SECRET

CENTRAL INTELLIGENCE AGENCY | DIRECTORATE OF INTELLIGENCE
Subject: Lack of Leadership among Rebel Factions

It is unquestionable that the Indonesian populace have no love lost with the current government under Sukarno, his heavy-handed policies exploiting the rural provinces at their expense while his favoritism has led to growing divisions among most branches of government. More to the fact is that many see the government as a mere puppet to Tokyo, its creeping influence felt in both the industrial sector and within its armed forces.

Yet, even despite this unifying cause for revolt, no leader among the rebelling factions have proven capable to truly bring together the full force of Sukarno's opposition. Each group differs too greatly in their objectives and aims, which leaves the prospect of a popular/ elite-driven coalition against the regime a remote possibility, for the time being.

We will continue to monitor the situation, until new developments arise.
strings.USA_INS.103.desc:
CLASSIFICATION: TOP SECRET

CENTRAL INTELLIGENCE AGENCY | DIRECTORATE OF INTELLIGENCE
Subject: Contact with PDAF Leader

After various attempts of reaching, let alone finding the man in charge of the People's Democratic Armed Forces, our operatives have been able to make contact with the elusive head of this socialist rebel group: Amir Sjafruddin.

Despite the PDAF's evident need for our support, Sjafruddin has been quite skeptical in accepting any form of proposition from us, no doubt because of his ideological background. We may be able to persuade him by presenting our concrete aid to the UMAJF in Malaya, to ease any doubts about our commitment.

We will report any further developments when they arise.
strings.USA_INS.104.desc:
CLASSIFICATION: TOP SECRET

CENTRAL INTELLIGENCE AGENCY | DIRECTORATE OF INTELLIGENCE
Subject: Several Agents Compromised

Following the recent declaration of martial law by Sukarno and the full nationalization of Japanese assets across the country, we regret to inform you that several of our informants, plus one handler, had been compromised due to the ongoing chaos, resulting in their arrest by local security forces. However, much to our surprise, they had approached us with an offer.

One Zulkifli Lubis, the director of the Indonesian Intelligence Directorate, had proposed that in return for broader support of the rebel groups situated in the Sumatra region, our agents would be released from captivity. It is truly fortunate for us to have made an ally in such high ranking within the government, and we have taken the appropriate measures to make use of this golden opportunity.

It should be stated in the record, however, that luck is far from an actionable policy for our profession.
strings.USA_INS.105.desc:
CLASSIFICATION: TOP SECRET

CENTRAL INTELLIGENCE AGENCY | DIRECTORATE OF INTELLIGENCE
Subject: Status Report on Indonesian Crisis

The sweeping chaos following the recent introduction of martial law, along with the nationalization of major Japanese corporate assets, has brought a spike of unpopularity to the Sukarno regime, with dissent rising even among the government's own ranks in response to this heavy-handed shift of policy. Among them is the one remaining political figure that remains respected by the Indonesian populace: the Vice-President, Mohammad Hatta.

According to intel on the ground, Hatta has expressed great opposition to the recent policies implemented by Sukarno, as well as being noted to have grown far more distant with his revolutionary friend than he had been before. Due to his unblemished standing among the public eye, we believe that we may have finally found the rallying figure to kickstart the rebellion into action.

The Agency advises to attempt reaching out to Vice-President Hatta, directly if possible but more likely by approaching him through either rebel groups in Sumatra or Sulawesi. Through his public standing, he will become the figurehead of a self-sustaining movement capable of opposing Sukarno proper.
strings.USA_INS.106.desc:
CLASSIFICATION: TOP SECRET

CENTRAL INTELLIGENCE AGENCY | DIRECTORATE OF INTELLIGENCE
Subject: Ongoing Shipments of Weapons to Rebel Forces

Our operatives in the Special Activities Division, alongside those of the Australian Secret Intelligence Service, have resumed the shipment of weaponry towards the Permesta rebel groups situated in North Sulawesi via the Arafura Sea, as well as to rebel forces situated in West Sumatra through Sri Lanka. Through the use of intermediaries, we have been able to avoid detection by Indonesian patrol boats, as well as avoiding the recently-dispatched fleets from the Imperial Japanese Navy.

Despite the precautions, we have noted that several shipments of armaments haven't reached their expected timeframe and have gone missing. We do not doubt the possibility that some of these shipments have been waylaid during their crossing by unknown third parties, but we believe such losses to be minimal in importance compared to an airtight operational security.

We will maintain further reports on the situation.
strings.USA_INS.200.desc:
In a cold room somewhere in the vast halls of the Department of State is a large table littered with maps and drawings and printouts. Crowding around that table are men in dark suits, packed in closely to listen, and all across the room their faces are serious, their minds fully focused on the task at hand. Smith - the Department Head for International Security Affairs - was at the front, looking most serious of all and ready to begin this morning's briefing.

“Thank you for coming today. I believe all of you have seen the recent statements from the Australian government calling for a full-scale intervention,” Smith began. “Since they're on the front pages of every single newspaper in this country.”

“I'd like to take the opportunity to clear up our department's official position. While we appreciate their enthusiasm, we will not recommend a direct intervention in Indonesia.”

Scattered murmurs fluttered around the room: some of the stony faces showed flashes of concerns. Would America be wobbly at a time of great need?

“Make no mistake: we are just as committed to the war as the Australians are. This position may even change in the future. But we understand that escalating the war so quickly comes with risks that are far too high to bear. To put it bluntly, we risk war with Japan itself.” That seemed to quieten the room, and Smith continued.

“This is not to say that we will not be escalating the conflict - we will, but gradually. I trust you will do a good job of making sure the Australians know that.” Smith was almost done, now, and the men were ready to leave. As they prepared to go to their tasks, Smith had one final message.
strings.USA_INS.200.a: “Remember: slow and steady wins the race.”
strings.USA_INS.201.desc:
“Hello and good morning. Can I speak to Colonel Joop Warouw? This is Agent Thompson - I'm from the CIA.”

There continued to be no response for some time, even after Thompson waited what felt like a few minutes, so he wondered whether he'd got the wrong number after all. This task was important enough to wait, however.

If America was to win in Indonesia, it needed connections, and there wasn't anyone in North Suwalesi that was more pro-OFN than Colonel Warouw. So he continued to wait patiently, hearing the shuffling of chairs and some muffled conversation in the background.

A young man's voice suddenly came on the line: it spoke in clean, slightly accented English. “This is the Colonel's translator. Who are you?”

Thompson was startled, but quickly gathered himself. “Ah, yes, thank you. I'm Agent Thompson. CIA. We've been monitoring the situation in your country for some time: all of America is impressed by your movement's courage and strength.

”I want to let you know that we have your back all the way. We'll be sending you supplies by air and submarine: you should get them soon. This should help you to hold your ground against Suharto's regime. If you ever need anything, just call this number and we'll see what we can do for you.“

There was another pause before the young man spoke again. ”The Colonel thanks you greatly for your generous help. We promise that your help will not be in vain. Let's stay in touch.“

They chatted for a little while after that, exchanging some pleasantries, before breaking it off. And as Agent Thompson walked back to his home in the dead of night, he felt a tremendous sense of satisfaction at another day's work done.
strings.USA_INS.201.a:
We've done our part, he thought.
Now it's up to them.
strings.USA_INS.202.desc:
It was a rather understated opening, in truth. Only a smattering of officers, no more than fifty, were gathered in the shade on plastic chairs, ready for the proceedings to begin. This relatively modest affair - on a small field in Sumatra - belied the importance of what was about to happen. This event was the grand opening of the very first branch of MACI-SOG, the Special Operations Group of the Military Assistance Command Indonesia.

The General went to the stage, tapped the mic, then began speaking from a set of prepared remarks. “Thank you all for coming today. It is my honor to inaugurate this fine command.

”MACI-SOG's primary purpose is to train the brave Free Indonesian soldiers so that they can win this war. We will make sure that the Free Indonesians will receive the best instruction they can: as such, we will be training them directly.“

He paused for a moment. ”Our second purpose is to organize our forces. This command's responsibility is to ensure that our intervention is effective.“

”This command is a powerful sign. It shows to our allies - and our enemies - America's firm and total commitment to the war. In fact, to show this commitment“ the General said, gesturing to the crowd. ”This branch will not be our only one. Two more branches will be established soon, one on Sulawesi and the other on West Papua.“

That line garnered polite applause. Smiling, he continued with his final lines.
strings.USA_INS.202.a: “America isn't going away. You can be sure of that.”
