In fact, nothing about the flat, robotic speech of the junior attaché as they read through the press release that the U.S embassy in Caracas had hastily prepared to congratulate the Venezuelan government in its triumph against the communist threat rang like any triumph at all.

Its sole flavor was of the same weariness that was reflected upon the faces of each attendee, clearly unmoved by all the hollow praises of their success in “restoring national stability.”

One that was also found in the soldiers, advisors, liaison officers, and other American personnel who were now packing their meager belongings after having spent one last, joyless night in the air base. Packing plain crates in solemn quiet. Hoping to avoid the gaze of the Venezuelan troops stationed on the other side of the perimeter fence. Likely in fear of what they might spot in it.

Not that there would have been much of note to find. No hint of the hate they'd expect, nor of anything else, really, other than the same fatigue they all shared. There was nothing to say, nothing to shake hands on, and especially nothing to remember from operations that, officially, had never existed at all, and never would.

Perhaps a stubborn few would nonetheless try to cling to a handful of keepsakes. Maybe some crude patch bearing the Venezuelan flag that they'd bought for a buck or two from some unremarkable street vendor in the slums. For most, however, their only wish was to forget and move on.

And if some on the other side harbored fear that the Americans would never truly leave, observing the last helicopters fade into tiny dots amidst the Caribbean skyline at least provided some measure of solace.
strings.USA_VEN.33.a: And soon, it would be as if nothing had ever even occurred.
strings.USA_VEN.34.desc:
CONFIDENTIAL/{date}

From: Office of Central American Affairs
Memorandum for the Director
SUBJECT: INCREASED ACTIVITY FROM VENEZUELA'S ARMED FORCES OF NATIONAL LIBERATION

1. There has been a significant uptick in activity from the Fuerzas Armadas de Liberación Nacional (FALN), a communist guerrilla organization. Domestic turmoil, combined with victories for the FALN, has given it a much stronger profile, and much of Venezuela's eastern, Amazonian, and Andean territories are under their control, while students and urban workers offer a broader support base.

2. This conflict has been monitored with increasing focus, but the true scale of this insurgency has only recently become clear. A raid on student dormitories in the Central University of Venezuela in Caracas has revealed a sizable presence and backing for the UTC, an urban terror movement associated with FALN, and has coincided with a series of bombings against local military posts.

3. Disrupting the FALN should be considered, and is still possible for now. Aid to the Venezuelan government would likely need to be more substantial than a few bullets, but even a small troop deployment should be feasible without much backlash, save from Havana. Alternatively, the Venezuelan government still seems capable of responding to the FALN, and it might be wisest to save our diplomatic and military strength for larger targets.
strings.USA_VEN.34.a: The choice rests in your hands.
strings.USA_VEN.34.tt: Opportunities to meddle in the ongoing South American crises can be found in the Intelligence Tab.
strings.USA_VEN.35.desc:
In a plain building of fading stucco east of Plaza Altamira, a cluster of men looked around a map of Venezuela pinned up to a peeling wall. These men, field officers, intelligence analysts, and attachés, alternatively took drags of their cigarettes and pointed things out on the map.

One man grunted. “The leftist insurgency has been steadily gaining power in recent months. Rumors and whispers were one thing, a slogan spray-painted in an alley could be something or just some kid with more balls than sense, but pamphlets in the barrios are increasing. 'Join us in the Andes.' 'Take back your country.' 'Be the hidden hand of liberation.' We can't ignore this.”

“They're getting bolder,” another man with the stout neck that marked him as an infantry officer commented. “More strikes against armories and granaries. It's one thing to burn them down, but when you break it and steal it, it's because you need it. Their training camps have at least a third more mouths to feed and hands to fill with guns now, I'm certain.”

“Then we need to take action. We need to decide exactly what course of action we'd take and what level of intervention we'd need to keep our involvement at. We can just wage a simple information war, fight pamphlets with pamphlets. Otherwise, we could attempt to hit their critical lifelines. Their leaders are well-protected, but if we expose the people that the leftists depend on - supply drivers, message couriers, pamphleteers - we let them be arrested, and the movement withers. Otherwise, if we want to go full scorched-earth, we'll need to do something massive and find a way to blame the leftists, galvanizing popular support against them.”
strings.USA_VEN.35.a: A simple information war. Expose leftist atrocities and corruption within FALN with leaflets in the barrios.
strings.USA_VEN.35.b: Expose mid-level figures, propagandists, and couriers for arrest, and if necessary, arrange a few “accidents.”
strings.USA_VEN.35.c: No half-measures. Arrange a bombing on an oil pipeline and release information to publicly accuse FALN.
strings.USA_VEN.36.desc:
The rust-red bricks and fading tin defined the buildings of Caracas's cerros. Petare was the largest slum in Caracas by population, and those faded and collapsing walls held a rich tapestry of the misery of human poverty. Yet even still, life went on, and when people could, they tried to lend a hand with whatever meager power they possessed. A small clinic operated at all hours, with two overworked doctors helped by an assortment of middle-aged midwives, medically-discharged soldiers using first-aid training, and priests providing semi-professional mental health counseling. Two men, undercover agents for the FBI, took a break from setting a broken bone to discuss the next element of their strategy.

“This clinic isn't just preserving lives. Every illness we treat and broken bone we set is a victory over the guerrillas. They say that they serve the people, but they're not the ones driving food and vitamins into the barrios. They preach that the Church must be exterminated, but the Church faithful are the ones who actually put in the hours here. This is what we need to do to discredit them, show them that this is the better way. Once the word gets out, the people they claim to be fighting for will give them up.”

“In a decade maybe! The reason why the guerrillas get support is that their message is simple. Nothing is your fault; everything bad in your life is the work of the nefarious Yanqui. You're always going to find suckers who eat that garbage up. We need to work fast, get the word out that these people are monsters. If we can produce materials about them provoking attacks as false flags, that will win over the people in a heartbeat.”

“We have to give a report soon. Washington is going to want a tangible next step. Do we pressure the government to devote more money to the clinic, or do we go for the throat?”
strings.USA_VEN.36.a: “Keep the clinic working and the food aid flowing. People will believe in a government that works for its people.”
strings.USA_VEN.36.b: “Go aggressive. Make inroads with opposition newspapers and plant salacious rumors to get people to turn on the guerrileros.
strings.USA_VEN.37.desc:
From the rest of the crowd he was indistinguishable, a nobody in a sea of nobodies just buying an empanada. Maybe he was on his lunch break, maybe it was his day off. One wouldn't expect him to be a terrorist, certainly not Frank.

Frank sat in the back of a stuffy hot van in Caracas, surrounded by three other sweaty FBI agents. They were hunting Gustavo Montoya, an urban coordinator who had orchestrated a bombing in a cafe a week prior. At least Frank thought it was. He was brought on a few days ago after one of the agents was killed. Conrad, the new lead, was briefing him.

“Now, the guy in the black there,” he pointed to a man approaching Gustavo, “is gonna hand him a photo.”

“What's the photo of?” Frank asked.

“It's his family. It doesn't really matter much. From there he'll either follow our man there, or we'll chase. He might also try shooting. Either way he's trapped. Now, just watch.”

Just as Conrad said, the man handed Gustavo a photo and walked away with his hand in his pocket. Gustavo stood, looking at the photo for a while, before acting.
strings.USA_VEN.37.a: He walks with the man in black, and enters a police station. No one will hear of him again. Frank and Conrad will go on to someone else.
strings.USA_VEN.37.b: Gustavo tries to run. Guns are drawn and badges are pulled out. Cameras flash as he's handcuffed.
strings.USA_VEN.38.desc:
The envelope felt like a weight in his hand as he rode in the back of the wagon along with his three other companions. Santiago's men were a deniable ops team headed toward an idyllic village in provincial Barinas. Across the great plains of the state, the men herded goats while the children played by chasing dragonflies in the marshlands that lined its numerous rivers. The people there were largely apathetic toward national life and the vagaries of politics and simply kept to themselves. A few would go into town, with trucks of animals to sell to butchers, to bring back salt, medicine, and other modern essentials that the rich land couldn't provide for itself. They paid their taxes, but otherwise, the village abided and let the nation abide around them. It was perfect, and thus, the perfect backdrop for a terrible crime.

He had been paid handsomely to do deniable operations for the United States for years. Santiago had simply never fit in anywhere else: he wasn't violent but never felt right at peace, and the thought of a job working standard hours bored him to tears. His father worked himself to the bone for a pittance, and that gave Santiago the feeling that he would always need more. The Yanquis could provide more in three months than he'd earn in six years. The insurgents would kill for a man like him, but they could never afford him - they'd pay him in promises when the Yanquis gave him gemstones, the currency of the man who didn't exist.

The envelope would have the mission outline. Santiago knew that this envelope contained what he was to do, and what this village would see. The goal would be to de-legitimize the leftists, blaming them for a terrible atrocity. Santiago knew that they would probably do it, sooner or later, but this way, his paymasters could spin it and keep him flush. He opened the envelope, got his lighter ready to burn it, and read the contents.
strings.USA_VEN.38.a: Keep things clean. Burn a grain silo and run the story that this neutral town was attacked for refusing to support the leftists.
strings.USA_VEN.38.b: Massacre the village, release photos of guerrillas who were refused by town leaders. Let the world know that they are monsters.
strings.USA_VEN.39.desc:
The safehouse meeting in the warehouse in Santa Bárbara del Zulia was barely that more welcoming than anything else in Venezuela. Ever since Gustavo Machado and the FALN took power, red militias had been skulking around in every urban center and on every country road for infiltrators. Cutting the head off the leadership in Caracas and sending the communists into political infighting was going to be tricky in this environment, but this was the least Washington could do to kneecap Caracas and cut America's losses in the Andes.

“So? Just shoot the old fart then!” The Condor Legion's point-man, Uruguayan and 21, was a blithering fascist idiot, but at least his aim was decent. “Give me a few weeks to scout out the parade route, Machado will never see it coming and most of the Venezuelan military won't either.” Training a sniper team to attack the president in the open was maybe a bit too straightforward, but maybe that was all they needed.

“Explosives could do the job just as well.” The Condor Legion's commander, Colombian and 25, was even worse, talked big and liked to plan big. “Charges along the motorcade route can be hidden out of sight, take Machado out that way.” Bombing the motorcade was likely to come with additional casualties, but had a much better chance at killing Machado outright.

The FBI Station Chief rolled his eyes, adjusted his glasses: “What about something up close, poison maybe?” He scratched his head. “Somebody on his staff we can lean on, put something in his food, maybe pull something during one of his hospital visits?” Machado was like a lot of leaders in that stress equaled health issues needing regular check ups. It was a bit old hat, but history showed that it could be done.
strings.USA_VEN.39.a: Train a sniper team to take Machado out.
strings.USA_VEN.39.b: Plant a bomb along the motorcade.
strings.USA_VEN.39.c: Have a third party that can get closer to him.
strings.USA_VEN.40.desc:
The afternoon sun beat down on the Plaza O'Leary as men of the Condor Legion's cell spied the surrounding area below, just as they had done almost every day across every rooftop they had access to and even a few they legally didn't. They kept a low profile in this process, taking in the view of the Plaza as they settled on a rooftop that offered overwatch, sharing beers while reviewing notes on nearby escape routes and Machado's itinerary, trying to key in the timing for the fatal shot they both knew was coming.

The FBI attaché scanning the Plaza below was tabulating the options available for the operation. Particularly, how to handle the most important part of the plan: The shooter. American intelligence was no stranger to political assassination and even less so to sharpshooter-based geopolitics, but the potential for this to backfire was far too real for Quantico's liking and preferred some assurances that it was going to go their way.

Relying on Condor Legion to be the shooter was iffy at best, giving the FBI just enough believable distance to cover their rear. That said, all the cover in the world didn't mean much if the bullet missed its mark. There was the option of having the FBI supply one of their own professional shooters to be on the marquee for Machado operation, but while that yielded a better chance for the assassination to go through, there was very little wiggle room if things went bust, especially if it was one of their guys left holding the bag.
strings.USA_VEN.40.a: Set up one of the FBI's agents in the sniper's role.
strings.USA_VEN.40.b: Let Condor Legion do what they're here to do.
strings.USA_VEN.41.desc:
The car shop in Petare was a place of pride once upon a time, maybe it still was, just for different reasons. The owner had all but wept in pleading with Condor Legion about the true nature of his business, knowing full well that the many communist sympathizers in the area wouldn't be sympathetic to the local explosives workshop was in dealings with the infamous international “fascistas de mierda”. The bribe that the Station Chief had provided to ensure his cooperation doubtless alleviated some of his fears.

The Condor Legion's plan had acquired the device for the upcoming operation; high-grade plastic explosive satchel charges, intermediate blast radius, enough to blow Machado's limousine sky high before the motorcade could realize. Placing the bomb under a traffic median would work well-enough to disguise the device from sight long enough for the motorcade to pass near it. This method was cleaner, but there was no pretending Machado was not the victim of a political assassination.

This was what informed the other option that came with it, one that had a heavy price attached. Planting the bomb on a fuel tanker carried via truck and arranging it to be in the motorcade's path would make it believably look like an accident, but would very likely put bystanders in the blast zone. It would give Washington and the FBI some cover, but how necessary is the loss of life for optics?
strings.USA_VEN.41.a: The bomb will be rigged on the fuel truck, take no chances.
strings.USA_VEN.41.b: A precision bomb is enough, minimize the loss of life to Machado.
strings.USA_VEN.42.desc:
Not all of the political establishment in Venezuela went the way of the Dodo when the reds took Caracas, even the most diehard communist can make a concession for a true believer in the cause. Failing that, they can make exceptions for someone loud enough, desperate enough or lucky enough to ride the tiger just long enough not get eaten themselves.

There's a young nurse at the private clinic that services Gustavo Machado regularly who can attest to this first hand, her father being a URD senator who dipped his flag for the FALN after the Revolution. All's fair in love and war, even in class war as it turns out. Maybe that's how his daughter got such a prestigious job, working in close proximity with the president, a perfect opportunity to slip something lethal into whatever cocktail Machado's doctors are mixing for him.

If her father's decision making was any indication, maybe the daughter could be brought around in a similar fashion. The assassination was geared to throw the establishment into turmoil as multiple figures in the FALN tried to fill Machado's shoes, the kind that would likely see class traitors like the senator targeted first by a lot of the hardliners during the chaos. Offering asylum in the US to the nurse and her family could mollify this fear, so long as she plays along.

That having been said, it might be worthwhile to play hardball. You can never know someone's commitment until they're put under pressure and for all we know the woman and her father are true believers in the FALN, this might require a heavy hand just to make sure. The reality of the 'threat posed' by the Condor Legion was something very different, but the idea of the threat they would pose for her family might be enough to frighten her into cooperating.
strings.USA_VEN.42.a: Convince her. If her father served democracy, she can too, and be rewarded for it.
strings.USA_VEN.42.b: Threaten her. If the reds don't get to her loved ones, the Condor Legion will...
strings.USA_VEN.43.t: Gone in A Puff of Smoke
strings.USA_VEN.43.desc:
Agent Silverado Pérez took one gulp of the rum for himself, coughing as the cheap rotgut burned his throat. The rest of the bottle was being poured into a trashcan with a lifetime's worth of files. Every correspondence with the Condor Legion, every supply shipment, every complaint about the perennially malfunctioning toilet, all dumped into a can that had doubled as a barbecue pit just yesterday.

Machado was dead, but that was only the beginning of the nightmare for Venezuela. During Machado's state funeral, a bomb placed in a trash can ripped through the assembled people. It was a small-yield bomb, but it had caused the crowd to surge forward. The poorly-trained paramilitary forces panicked, opening fire on the crowd with live weapons. Naturally, the people ran in an attempt to save themselves and trampled each other in an attempt to get away. Hundreds more perished, either from gunfire, from trampling, or just being in the wrong place at the wrong time. One man's death seemed to echo again and again.

In the halls of power, the Revolutionary Council turned on each other. Everyone and their mother was accused of soliciting foreign support: the Gringos, the Germans, the Japanese, the Mexicans, the Brazilians, it didn't matter. Emergency votes and demands for internal inquiries were flying freely in Caracas's capital, and the factions began mobilizing their street armies to protect their enclaves from rival attacks. Already, whispers of alliances and intrigue abounded as each sought to secure themselves in the chaotic aftermath.

“Mission accomplished.” Silverado braved one more quaff of the fiery brew, then tossed the bottle in the can. He took a match from the box, lit the rest still in their cardboard confines, then tossed the whole package in. Between the rum and the fuel already in the bottom, the evidence would burn quickly. Silverado turned away as the blaze spurted to life and looked forward to his next posting.
strings.USA_VEN.43.a: The FBI's fires burned, just one more fire in a country aflame, and the Condors swooped into the night.
strings.USA_VEN.44.desc:
Agent Silverado Pérez took another drink of the cheap rum, hoping that it would cure his headache. The damn fools in the Condor Legion had botched what was supposed to be a routine operation. The old bastard had survived, even had the strength to gloat about it the next day. He saw it on the television, with children waving red flags as he, leaning on the balcony to support him, proclaimed his survival as a testament to the tenacity of his revolutionary spirit. “Make no mistake, the gringos fear what we have done here. They fear a people's victory and will stop at nothing to silence it. That should embolden all of us to continue our path, to continue to see the gringos quake in the wake of the people's victory.”

Pérez would have thrown a bomb at the smug bastard if he weren't surrounded by so many human shields. It was a mistake trusting those unprofessional pesky fascist teenagers. They had local connections that he lacked, but could do nothing with them. Incompetents, the lot of them, all they did was expose themselves and leave them open for an inevitable retaliation. Now they were being hunted, and Silverado knew it was only a matter of time before someone gave up American involvement. Few would actually believe it - Machado was already speaking about American involvement in everything from accidents at oil refineries to bad weather. The people who believed it would have already believed it; the people who didn't wouldn't trust a mere confession extracted after pulling a few molars.

Still, the revolution had hardened itself in the wake of its first trial, a true baptism by fire. They could unite themselves in that they were attacked and survived. The mark of any true revolutionary movement was enduring the reactions that followed. That meant his time in Venezuela was at an end. With the Condor Legion being hunted on the streets, Silverado had an opportunity. By the time any hint of his agency would be murmured, he'd be long gone. Leave the failures to reap the consequences, and he would simply vanish into the night.
strings.USA_VEN.44.a: A lifetime to build, a moment to have it all slip away.
strings.USA_VEN.45.desc:
It was stifling in the conference room of the “Gran Hotel Ancira” in Monterrey, even though the ceiling fans were running at their limit, slicing through the humid Mexican air. This location was chosen specifically: close enough to Texas to be convenient for the Americans, but far enough from Caracas not to taunt the Iberian hawks.

Eugenio Mendoza sat at the table with a straight back. He wore an impeccable light linen suit that distinguished him from everyone else in the room. He was a civilian to the bone - a philanthropist, a businessman, a man of numbers.

Opposite sat the American delegation. They smiled at Mendoza. They knew his name, they knew his reputation. With him, one could speak of dividends and charitable foundations. But their eyes kept sliding to the space behind Mendoza.

There, against the wall, sat the generals. Throughout the entire meeting, they did not utter a single word. Their uniforms were buttoned to the top, despite the heat. The Military Depoliticization Act had been signed just a week ago; the ink on it was fresh, but confidence in it was even thinner than the paper itself. The Americans saw hope in Mendoza, but in the generals, they saw a threat.

The “Monterrey Protocol” lying on the table was a masterpiece of diplomatic minimalism. No loud words about an “eternal alliance.” No military bases. Just dry points: supply guarantees, technical maintenance of pipelines, sharing of “low-level” intelligence. It was a document that could be hidden in a desk drawer if Iberia started asking questions.

Mendoza unscrewed the cap of his pen, recalling the rule he had derived while building the “Vencemos” empire: the strongest cement takes a long time to cure. In 1958, when he was part of the Junta, they tried to build democracy too quickly, and the structure cracked.
strings.USA_VEN.45.a: Now, he did not intend to repeat that mistake.
strings.USA_VEN.45.tt:
The {usa_getflag} United States will only be able to claim {ven_getflag} Caracas if {ibr_getflag} Madrid loses its foothold in the {col_getflag} Northern Andes and we regain our rightful place as the region's hegemon.

For now, though, relations with the {ven_getflag} Venezuelan government will remain open.
strings.USA_VEN.46.desc:
CONFIDENTIAL/{date}

FROM KEVIN RAWLINGS
MEMORANDUM FOR THE U.S DEPARTMENT OF STATE

SUBJECT: OVERTHROW OF VENEZUELAN GOVERNMENT BY GENERAL JESÚS MARÍA CASTRO LEÓNn

Following an election that resulted in a left-wing government being put in power, self-exiled former Venezuelan Air Force General Jesús María Castro León has overthrown the government in the so-called “Easter Coup”. Rallying barracks to his cause, he was able to quickly march to Caracas from the Colombian border while taking minimal casualties. Upon taking control, Castro León announced a policy called the “Five National Points,” focused on reconstruction of Venezuela after recent turmoil and the creation of a constitution that gives the military more power.

Despite these lofty goals, contacts within the new government have reported that General Castro León is in ill health, and has been delegating more and more duties to Eugenio Mendoza, a business tycoon, and Colonel Moncada Vidal, the minister of internal affairs and Castro León's military protégé. The coup marks a change in Venezuelan foreign policy, with a harsh shift from the Veracruz Pact to the Iberian Union's sphere of influence. Most consequential is Castro León's reluctant anti-American beliefs. Due to his ailing health, contacts recommend getting in touch with Mendoza, a more moderate figure in the government.
strings.USA_VEN.47.desc:
CONFIDENTIAL/{date}

FROM GEOFFREY MACFAYDEN
MEMORANDUM FOR THE U.S DEPARTMENT OF STATE

SUBJECT: COMPLETION OF THE “FIVE NATIONAL POINTS” IN VENEZUELA, MENDOZA TAKES POWER

Jesús María Castro León has announced in an address in Caracas that the “Five National Points” have been completed and that he will be retiring before the end of the year. Contacts in the government speculate either his rapidly failing health or a genuine commitment to the government. The address was met with mostly positive press, although this may have been because of press censorship.

Taking leadership is the National Governing Board, a body of the nation's most important families, tycoons and technocrats, which is watched closely by the military. The leader of the board is the richest man in Venezuela and a reluctant associate of Castro León, Eugenio Mendoza. A philanthropist and believer in the social responsibilities of businesses, contacts within the government have said that Mendoza is preparing the nation for democratization, only accepting Castro León's proposal to prevent a more radical alternative from taking power and secure a stable future for Venezuela and her people.

This process has only received tepid support from the board members, with Pedro Tinoco being the leader of the opposition. The military also remains in fierce opposition to the process. Considering the current situation in Venezuela, Mendoza is the best option for American interests, especially when considering the radical Bolivarianists represented by Moncada Vidal.
strings.USA_VEN.48.desc:
NATIONAL INTELLIGENCE ESTIMATE
THE PROBLEM

Venezuela's long period of chaos is over, and it has reemerged as a democratic society, an American ally, and a place to do business. Eugenio Mendoza has successfully fended off threats from within the National Governing Board and the Army to enact his reformist agenda. Elections are set for 1970, which merits monitoring to ensure this newfound stability persists.

Conclusions

1- Eugenio Mendoza took power in the wake of a period of political turmoil at the head of the National Governing Board, an assembly of Venezuela's most powerful oligarchs with, initially, heavy influence from the Armed Forces, united by a desire to secure their interests by any means necessary. Mendoza cut an unusual figure among this group, as its most powerful member and a liberal democrat. The Board immediately set about stabilizing Venezuela, largely by stamping out political violence with state power.

2- Mendoza faced opposition from two powerful groups: The so-called “desarrollistas”, led by board member and magnate Pedro Tinoco, who advocated maintaining emergency powers indefinitely and enriching themselves via state corruption, and two dissident factions within the military: the Bolivarianists led by Colonel Moncada Vidal and the Perezjimenistas, primarily led by Luis Felipe Llovera Páez. Mendoza crippled the former with corruption investigations and deftly purged the latter. With his position secure, Mendoza declared the Board's purpose fulfilled and a restoration of democracy necessary.

3- Mendoza has ensured Venezuela will remain in our orbit. His actions have ensured the country will remain our strongest ally in the Caribbean, but also a stable and prosperous nation with a democratic future. Yet a nascent democracy is a playground for radicals and malcontents. We must remain vigilant.
strings.USA_VEN.49.desc:
NATIONAL INTELLIGENCE ESTIMATE

THE PROBLEM

Venezuela has left behind both the recent catastrophes and its tentative democratic tradition. The National Governing Board, composed of the country's most prominent oligarchs, has ousted its liberal head, Eugenio Mendoza, in favor of the dictatorial Pedro Tinoco. Tinoco will return Venezuela to democracy, however elections will be tightly controlled and vested interests' power never to be relinquished.

Conclusions

1- Using the connections gained during his period running an elite Caracas law firm, Pedro Tinoco attained a position as Managing Director of the Banco Mercantil, solidifying himself among the capital's elite. Tinoco began his political career under the dictatorship of Juan Gómez, and it was then that he began building up the basis for what would be his faction.

2- Pedro Tinoco leads the “Desarrollista” faction, which advocates primarily for maintaining corporate oligarchy, strident anti-Communism, and developmentalist policies to be fueled by the country's massive oil wealth. Opposed to Mendoza's democratic instincts from the very start, Tinoco undermined him everywhere, but especially in his efforts to curb his faction's corruption. The Desarrollistas resistance paid off, forcing Mendoza to retire, and exalting Tinoco in his place.

3-Tinoco is a banker at heart and is primarily concerned with preserving his and his allies' wealth. He will implement a nominal democracy under his new party, Integración Republicana, and hold perfucntory, rigged elections. Nevertheless, Tinoco shall prevent the country from slipping into the control of anti-American radicals.
strings.USA_VEN.50.desc:
CONFIDENTIAL/{date}

FROM FBI DIRECTOR J.EDGAR HOOVER
MEMORANDUM FOR THE U.S DEPARTMENT OF STATE

SUBJECT: COLONEL JUAN DE DIOS MONCADA VIDAL SUCCEEDS CASTRO LEÓN IN VENEZUELA

Following the retirement of Castro León, close confidant and protégé Colonel Juan de Dios Moncada Vidal has succeeded him as president of Venezuela. Moncada Vidal is quite possibly the most anti-American figure in Venezuela and the worst possible outcome for our interests. Speeches and memoirs transcribed by contacts in the country reveal extreme nationalism and plans to expel American firms. Throughout his rise to power he has used violence extensively against his enemies, and it should be expected that he will use the same violence against American influence.

His faction of the military, calling itself the Bolivarianists, is an awkward blend of Julianos, soldiers inspired by the communist Porteñazo rebellion, Falangists, including members of the “Hitlerite Battalion,” and his personalist followers, who are extremely ideological, creating a unique rabidly nationalist fascist militarist ideology following a cult of personality around Venezuela's independence hero, Simón Bolívar. This mix of left and right politics have been united in their xenophobia, promises of national renewal as shown in the Five National Points, and anti-imperialist attitudes.

Despite his leftist support, he has been brutal in his repression of the domestic communist movement of Fuerzas Armadas de Liberación Nacional, leaving a weakened but radicalized core. With the FALN also staunchly anti-American, the best bet for returning American influence to Venezuela lies with the exiles who have fled to Mexico and the Sun Belt.
strings.USA_VEN.51.desc:
CONFIDENTIAL/{date}

FROM FBI DIRECTOR J.EDGAR HOOVER
MEMORANDUM FOR THE U.S DEPARTMENT OF STATE

The Republic of Venezuela, once one of our staunchest allies in Latin America, has transformed into a pernicious foe. Colonel Juan de Dios Moncada Vidal, a man who cuts a sinister and erratic figure, has led a coup reforming Venezuela into a Fascist dictatorship. The press has been prohibited from speaking out against the military regime, with disobedient opposition presses put to the torch, and countless others cowed into becoming regime mouthpieces. All parties besides the Colonel's own Bolivarian Military Civic Union have been outlawed.

Colonel Moncada Vidal has headlined his ambitious political program with the declaration of a “Bolivarian Republic”, a gesture rife with implications of Simón Bolívar's Gran Colombia that stretched from Ecuador to Essequibo. The move has dovetailed with the Colonel's dictatorial persona, loudly evocative of Bolívar. The Colonel has compared his own program of nationalization, militarization, and belligerence with the exploits of the eponymous General, and regime propaganda lauds him as a reincarnation of El Libertador.

Already, we have felt the consequences of the takeover: Americans in the country are harried by mobs, exiles have flooded our shores and newspaper columns, and oil and gold assets owned by American corporations have been seized and placed under the direct control of the military. Any response must be undertaken carefully, as the Colonel has launched a massive militarization campaign that has conscripted thousands of new soldiers, clear preparation for a possible intervention.

Yet, fissures within the regime and threats from outside manifest: Colonel Moncada Vidal's lieutenant, Hurtado Barrios, has flown his superior's coop and taken up with the leftist Julianos. Dissident forces within the country, the largest being the Communist FALN, have begun arming themselves. We can only hope they can do what we may be unable to.
strings.USA_VEN.52.desc:
CONFIDENTIAL/{date}

FROM FBI DIRECTOR J.EDGAR HOOVER
MEMORANDUM FOR THE U.S DEPARTMENT OF STATE

A transitional government has been declared by a military clique, led by Venezuela's former Caudillo, Marcos Pérez Jiménez. The new government has legitimacy, broad support, and a clear vision for the country, but the former dictator's predilections remain as worrying as they were in the 50s.

CONCLUSIONS

1-Marcos Jiménez was overthrown by Wolfgang Lazarrábal in 1958 for a variety of reasons, and, despite his regime being overall in our favor, we did next to nothing to prevent the coup. Pérez Jiménez had opened up the country to foreign investment, not only to our corporations, but to those closely tied to Fascist states as well. Pérez Jiménez clearly emulated these regimes in many ways, especially in his repressive methods in dealing with Communist rebels. He maintained a close relationship with Juan Domingo Perón in Argentina and attempted to craft a similar persona.

2-Following his overthrow, Pérez Jiménez went into exile in the Dominican Republic and subsequently Iberia, where he, by all accounts, only became more rabidly anti-Communist, telling associates that he would “do what he did before, only tenfold”. Directed by his secret police chief, Pedro Estrada, curfews, torture, public executions, and military occupation have already returned in force.

3-Jiménez's more positive policies are also echoes of his previous administration. We can expect him to implement the same New Deal-inspired, Keynesian policies as before. His primary focus appears to be infrastructure megaprojects like hydroelectric dams and highways. We recommend aiding him in his constructive measures and offering some aid in his anti-Communist crackdowns. We must make him dependent on our aid and our aid alone.
strings.USA_VEN.53.desc:
NATIONAL INTELLIGENCE ESTIMATE

THE PROBLEM

An attempt to restore Marcos Pérez Jiménez to power in Venezuela ended with him comatose, soon to be dead, and the nation in chaos. His daughter, Margot, has emerged out of the power vacuum as a puppet for the powerful secret police chief Pedro Estrada. The situation is unstable and subject to change.

Conclusions

1-Marcos Jiménez's attempt to retake power has ended in failure. While it is true that Jiménez acted against our interests in many ways, he nevertheless ensured stability. His daughter is a political nonentity, a puppet installed by regime elites, namely the Security Minister Pedro Estrada and General Laureano Vallenilla Planchart. Both men are ardent anti-Communists who have used extreme methods to eradicate the left from Venezuelan society.

2-The power bid by General Luis Llovera Páez, one of Jiménez's closest confidants and the obvious choice for a successor, was halted by Jiménez's death and the elevation of Margot. According to our sources, Páez believed that Jiménez would recover and therefore made none of the necessary steps to secure support within the ruling FEI party. We cannot discount the possibility that Jiménez was murdered not by the assassin's bullet, but by Margot's puppeteers. They stood to gain, and given Estrada's control over the hospitalized President, certainly had the opportunity.

3-The situation is changing as we speak. Forces within and outside the government are making moves; The countryside is aflame as the rebels take advantage of the chaos, and the new regime brutally counters them. The country is on the brink of Civil War. We must prepare for the worst.
strings.USA_VEN.55.desc:
CONFIDENTIAL/{date}

FROM FBI DIRECTOR J.EDGAR HOOVER
MEMORANDUM FOR THE U.S DEPARTMENT OF STATE

SUBJECT: NATIONAL INTELLIGENCE ESTIMATE ON VENEZUELAN SITUATION

While the outcome of Venezuela's recent coup may seem desirable on the surface, in reality, little has changed beyond the abeyance of outward aggression. The new regime has signaled hostility towards our government and has publicly refused to return our confiscated assets.

Conclusions

1-'The Dance of the Dogs,' as Caracas' top paper called it, is over. The regime of Colonel Moncada Vidal, by severing ties with us, set off a chain of events it could not control, which rocked the foundations of the Venezuelan economy and led to a surge of anti-state rebel activity. The dictatorship had no internal cohesion, with the Colonel's cabinet containing fractious personalities who constantly butted heads over trivialities. This led Hurtado Barrios, the Colonel's closest ally, to seek allies among the leftists in the military, namely Jesús Mollina Villegas and Pedro Medina Silva, to restore order.

2-Incensed by the chaos and increasingly despondent at Colonel Moncada Vidal's ability to fight it, Hurtado Barrios and his allies gathered forces and swiftly moved against the Colonel, overthrowing his regime and executing him. The new regime retains “Bolivarian” principles as a unifying ideology. Barrios has also proclaimed himself a Socialist, and many leftist guerrillas and exiles have reconciled with the new regime, though skepticism and resistance remain.

3-Nicolás Hurtado Barrios remains staunchly opposed to American interests in Latin America. It is advisable that we treat his government as a continuation of Colonel Moncada Vidal's dictatorship, and continue to aid Liberal Democratic forces within the country.
strings.USA_VEN.56.desc:
NEW HORIZON: WASHINGTON AND CARACAS SIGN “STABILITY PACT”
Minister Martín Vegas: “The Era of Uncertainty is Behind Us”

“...Yesterday at 11:00 PM, following a marathon of negotiations, the government officially announced the full normalization of relations with the United States. The agreement, which Minister of Foreign Affairs Vegas has already dubbed a 'return to hemispheric normalcy,' provides for the immediate opening of credit lines and security guarantees for our tankers in the Caribbean Sea.

Analysts note that the decisive factor was the recent 'pacification' of Colombia. With the end of the civil war on our borders, trade routes to the North are free once again, and Washington has unequivocally demonstrated who holds the keys to the Caribbean Basin.

In the corridors of Miraflores Palace, it is reported that the tone of the negotiations was strictly business. In the face of the looming global oil storm, Venezuela is choosing the most reliable home port. As a source close to President Tinoco remarked: 'We look at the map, and all arrows point North. To ignore this is to deny the fact that the Earth is round.'”
strings.USA_VEN.56.a: Vegas overdid it with the pathos, but the essence is correct.
strings.USA_VEN.56.tt:
With our recent victories in the Americas and the fading presence of {ibr_getflag} Iberia in the region, their {ven_getflag} Venezuelan partners have deemed it necessary to return to their rightful place, {usa_getflag} under the Eagle's wing.
------------------------------------
strings.USA_VEN.57.desc:
The familiar strains of the piano - Johann Sebastian Bach's “Jesu, Joy of Man's Desiring” - floated from television speakers across the country. This melody meant one thing: it was time to learn.

The familiar, ascetic image appeared on the screens: a writing desk, an “Electro-Voice” microphone, and a massive silhouette of Venezuela carved from dark wood on the wall. It loomed over Arturo Uslar Pietri like a silent judge.

The President sat motionless, hands clasped over a volume in a worn binding. He was not looking at the camera. He was staring into the void, as if seeing things inaccessible to the lens. “One hundred years ago,” he began quietly, “on the other side of the earth, there existed an empire that decided to stop time. They closed their ports. They banned foreign books. They believed their katana - the soul of the samurai - was stronger than any machine.”

Pietri finally raised his eyes. In the glare of the studio spotlights, his glasses glinted with cold steel. “And then the 'Black Ships' entered their harbor. Huge, smoking monsters of metal. And the proud empire realized a terrible truth: to save one's soul, one must learn to pilot the dragon's body. One cannot defeat a steam engine with verses about cherry blossoms.”

He slowly turned to the map behind his back. His shadow fell across the Orinoco Delta. “Some say that letting in foreign capital is dangerous,” Pietri turned and looked straight into the lens, as if peering into the soul of every viewer. “But was Peter the Great afraid of Dutch carpenters? Did he become less Russian when he built a fleet according to London's blueprints? No. And we, Venezuelans, face the same choice. We can sit proudly in the dark, or we can take the torch from the giant to light our own home.”

He smiled. “Do not be afraid to learn from the strong. Be afraid of remaining weak. Until next time on 'Valores Humanos'.”
strings.USA_VEN.58.t: Toast in the Hall of Mirrors
strings.USA_VEN.58.desc:
A bottle of “Grand Old Parr” whisky - squat and dark glass - stood on a low lacquered rosewood table. This whisky had been the unofficial currency of the Venezuelan elite since the 50s, and now Jóvito Villalba generously splashed the amber liquid into two massive tumblers.

The atmosphere in the Hall of Mirrors at Miraflores Palace was that of a meeting between old buddies. President Villalba was in his element. He paced the carpet, gesturing energetically with an unlit cigar.

“Leave that nonsense about 'imperialism' for the students on campus, Bob!” laughed Villalba, addressing US Ambassador Robert McClintock. “We live in the real world. As those Castro León and those who followed im demonstrated with the Easter Coup, democracy can't be just pretty words in the Constitution. It's working factories, full shelves, and, damn it, it's security!”

McClintock, sitting in his armchair with the relaxed confidence of a man backed by the Sixth Fleet, smiled. He liked Villalba. With this man, there was no need to play spy games. He wanted the same thing Washington did: to turn Venezuela into a showcase of the Western way of life in Latin America.

“Washington appreciates your enthusiasm, Mr. President,” the ambassador said, adjusting his cufflink. “President {usa_getpresidentlastname} believes that Caracas must become an anchor of stability. And we are ready to gild that anchor.”

“Precisely.” Villalba finally struck a match. “We give you the energy to keep your world spinning. You give us the shield to keep our world from collapsing. It's a fair deal.”

He raised his glass. The light of the massive crystal chandelier played in the facets of the glass.

“To partnership, Bob. Tell the White House: as long as we are here, Uncle Sam will always have a full tank and an open door. We are one family, and relatives must stick together.”
strings.USA_VEN.58.a: The Stars and Stripes goes perfectly with the Venezuelan tricolor.
strings.USA_VEN.59.t: The Shop Windows of Fifth Avenue
strings.USA_VEN.59.desc:
Dinner in the family dining room of the “La Casona” residence was coming to an end. For dessert, bienmesabe was served - a coconut cake Marcos loved but rarely ate, watching his figure. Today, he allowed himself an extra slice.

The atmosphere at the table was lively, quite unlike state receptions. “Daddy, so what about Saks?” Margot, the eldest daughter, who had recently turned twenty-four, tapped a manicured finger impatiently on the tablecloth. “The new catalog arrived a week ago, but Mom still isn't in the mood to look at it.”

Pérez Jiménez wiped his lips with a napkin and leaned back in his chair, unbuttoning his jacket, tailored in Madrid. “You can look,” he answered lazily. “And not just at the catalog.”

Doña Flor María, slicing the dessert with a silver fork, raised her eyebrows. “Was McClintock amenable?”

“McClintock was ready to lick the parquet floor, Flor,” Marcos chuckled. “They unfroze the accounts. All the accounts. The one at Chase Manhattan, and the trust fund in Florida.”

Florángel, the middle daughter, squealed with joy: “Does that mean we can go back to the house on Pine Tree Drive? I left my record collection there!”

“You can fly to Miami, to New York, even to Disneyland,” Pérez Jiménez swept his gaze over his women. “The Americans have given us, let's say... a 'platinum loyalty card.' They need my oil so badly that they are ready to turn a blind eye to anything. Want new fur coats? Buy them. Want to update the fleet? Order those Cadillacs you saw in the magazine.”

“But, daddy, what about the 'crimes of the regime'?” asked the second youngest, María Sol, sarcastically mimicking the intonation of American newscasters.

Marcos laughed - a rare, barking laugh, startling the youngest, Flor de María, named after her mother. “Well, darling. In Washington these days, crimes are forgiven if they are paid for with high-quality oil. So, Flor, book the tickets. I think it would be good for you all to get some fresh air and go shopping.”
strings.USA_VEN.59.a: On Uncle Sam's dime, of course.
strings.USA_VEN.60.desc:
CONFIDENTIAL/{date}

FROM THE VENEZUELA OFFICE OF THE FBI
MEMORANDUM FOR THE PRESIDENT

SUBJECT: MILITARY COUP IN VENEZUELA

1. Under the stated goal of ensuring national security in the face of the threat posed by the Fuerzas Armadas de Liberación Nacional, a rogue military faction has seized power in Venezuela in a bloodless coup. At the time of writing, all executive authority has been relinquished without any resistance from the now-deposed civilian administration and subsequently transferred to a provisional officer's junta helmed by General Pablo Antonio Flores.

2. With the former government having lost any public legitimacy it had retained after its disastrous response to the current civil war, it is expected that Antonio Flores' clique will remain in power for the foreseeable future. While far from an ideal outcome, an entrenched military regime should be regarded as a preferable alternative to any prospect of the communist guerrillas seizing lasting power over the country, as the latter case would assuredly lead to a complete severance of any diplomatic or commercial ties we may hope to maintain within Venezuela.

3. Accordingly, and despite the heightened hazard to the public perception of our ongoing operations in Latin America, we strongly urge our administration to offer the necessary resources and support for their continuation until the FALN threat is dealt with. Furthermore, it is believed Antonio Flores' junta could prove amenable to our position, and providing them with the breathing room to properly focus their efforts on the rebels could be just what they need to finally stabilize the situation in the fractured state...
strings.USA_VEN.60.a: ...starting with a public diplomatic overture to help them solidify their leadership.
strings.USA_VEN.60.b: ...as long as our logistical support remains covert and away from official channels.
strings.USA_VEN.60.c: ...but we trust them to handle it more than adequately without our direct interference.
strings.USA_VEN.68.desc:
Hundreds of miles from the leftover rubble and strained bureaucracy in Caracas, the powers that be in Venezuela prepared to hand back power to its native people. One end of a Pentagon conference room sat Enrique Tejera París and his soon-to-be cabinet, all that was left of the governing class after a bloody coup, a brutal dictatorship, a devastating civil war, and now, a global financial crisis threatening to tear down what remained. On the other sat a row of mostly American OFN generals, with President {getpresidentlastname} sitting at their head.

The leader of the OAS intervention himself, Rathvon Tompkins, spoke first in a gravelly voice. “Alright, Dr. París. Recent political and economic developments have caused us to expedite the nation-building process in Venezuela. Direct military administration is costing us forty million a week - this is unacceptable. We aim to formally announce the return to civilian governance shortly after this meeting. We have here a list of terms for your new government; you are welcome to make suggestions as you see fit.”

Tejera París nodded along - not that anything he could have said would matter, of course. The Americans already controlled their true prize - the gushing black rivers that were just about the most coveted thing in the world at the moment. With the economic downturn at home and military conflicts raging abroad, the costs of running the mandate directly were just weighing Washington down.

Tompkins pulled out a briefing and began reading. “Memorandum on the Transitional Period. Item 4, Paragraph B. OFN membership and continued OAS security presence. Uninhibited access to the Venezuelan oil trade. American oversight of political and security decisions...”

He droned on and on, but the point got through to Tejera París - despite the return of Venezuelans to their government, the Americans would still be the ones running the show. This was the only option, or else the Americans would surely be able to find someone less... scrupulous. No, all he could do now was agree to the American terms and prepare to be paraded about his own nation like a puppet on strings.
strings.USA_VEN.68.a: He mustered a smile, and gave his assent.
strings.USA_VEN.68.tt: ({ven_getflag} Venezuela)Though the occupation ends, with Dr. Enrique Tejera París rising to the seat of President of Venezuela, Venezuela will remain an American protectorate for many years to come.
strings.USA_VEN.69.t: Executive Report: The Venezuelan Interim Government
strings.USA_VEN.69.desc:
Director Hoover:

The OAS peacekeeping mission, including all troops stationed in Caracas and the Guyanese border region, has formed an interim government after the Venezuelan Civil War. Low-level insurgencies are active across both major cities and rural areas. Most of which are local fiefs operated by the old regime's commandants and caudillos. The administration is focused on re-establishing order in urban regions to construct the bureaucratic apparatus necessary for a planned post-transition election.

The former Venezuelan government's destruction has led to an increase in partisanship. Such a shift has since enabled a few pro-American contacts to gain political credibility. As a result of this newly formed network, future stabilization efforts, such as post-transition legislative actions, will have no significant opposition. However, many of them lack the capital to lobby without steady American funding, which limits their adherence to our doctrine by our capacity to afford their expenses. Similarly, many caudillos may also require such low-return investments to relinquish their fiefdoms for municipal governance.

Although there is a significant prospect of creating a functional nation from Venezuela's remains, it is, by and large, reliant on our willingness to support its unprofitable enterprise. If we opt to quell the states' decentralization with monthly payouts, our method might also create high levels of corruption. The reforms required to rectify such will cost about the same to implement. Unfortunately, without making Venezuela indebted to us, it is impossible for the OAS to patch up a junior partner out of the failed state.
strings.USA_VEN.69.a: In short, we made this problem for ourselves.
strings.USA_VEN_DONT_ATTACK_tt: It is advised that the OAS-OFN force stay on the defensive against Venezuela for the time being.
strings.USA_africa_riots.1.desc:
As the death count steadily increases, and more and more honest Americans mourn their loved ones, the political temperature is rising up at an alarming speed. After dozens of weekly reports from the FBI documenting ever-larger protests breaking out all throughout the country, now they are no longer needed to warn the government about the rising discontent, as the President himself found out today when he looked from the window of the White House.

Right before the gates to the Presidential Residence stood, grim and silent, dozens of men and women of all ages. Some held photos of husbands, children, brothers whose bodies - lost in the jungle or mangled beyond recognition - they couldn't even hold for a last goodbye, others posters decrying the “useless sacrifice” of human lives and accusing the “bloodthirsty capitalists” who “feed on death” to be the true force behind the government's decision to increase the draft.

The guards outside were visibly in difficulty: they surrounded the small crowd, but didn't try to dislodge them as they were unarmed and quiet. They didn't scream or try to force the block: they all waited there, and looked at a certain window, where a certain person was looking back. The President couldn't see their eyes, they were too distant for that, but he felt it: that cold, unwavering stare, full of hate and desire for vengeance made chills run down his spine.
strings.USA_africa_riots.1.a: We need to get a handle on this.
strings.USA_africa_riots.2.desc:
Day after day, the crowd waiting outside the White House increased steadily, until Lafayette Square was completely occupied by the silent protest. All around the United States, however, the manifestations are turning violent, as young college students who have been ensnared by extremist demagogues and radical politicians attack the police at their increasingly frequent gatherings.

The FBI reports have returned, but the tone is completely different: gone are “protests” and “discontent”, and for the first time, worrying words the likes of “resistance”, “terrorism” and “uprising” make their appearance. With more and more agents dispatched to monitor the growing opposition movements for signs of extremism, director Hoover is extremely worried about the future of the Union should this state of affairs not change.

One thing is certain: the President might refuse to open his windows to avoid looking outside, but the hate for the continued presense in Africa is growing. From colleges, where the deans report acts of vandalism, disobedience and secret meetings between students, to cities, with the police stretched thin to keep order, America is starting to fall apart at the seams. If we don't manage to end this war, one way or the other, there will be painful consequences. In the literal sense of the word.
strings.USA_africa_riots.2.a: Someone needs to do something about this.
strings.USA_africa_riots.3.desc:
All the windows of the White House are closed shut now, though “barricaded” would be more correct. After an armed assailant bypassed security and shot one of the presidential guards before being taken down by the others, an eerie atmosphere has taken over the staff, in stark contrast with the bright white of the walls: all personnel is screened before getting in, and the President has been de facto isolated in his office and private quarters.

All across the States, things are quickly getting out of hand. Extremism is spreading throughout the country like wildfire, demagogues and radicals spreading their lies and ideologies to everyone desperate or angry enough to listen to them. Those opposing our administration are united in their violent accusations: the President is a traitor to the United States for having sent tens of thousands of brave Americans to their deaths just to make the industrialists happy, they say. The administration is corrupted and ineffectual, and refuses to take the right choices for the good of all, they say. THEY will take all the right choices, they say.

The FBI is now too busy trying to douse the flames, and reports are curt, listing all the damage done, and what could even go worse. “If the war doesn't end NOW”, they all state, “the United States as we know it will be no more.”
strings.USA_africa_riots.4.desc:
The screams are deafening outside the White House. “Away with the President!” one yells, “Traitors! Murderers! Monsters!” an angry mother cries, clutching the photo of her only son as if it were a lifeline. “Bring the profiteers to court!” echoes her husband, angrily waving his poster. Day after day, the protests get worse. Chaos grips the capital, and the situation can only get worse. For once however, today the chaos outside the House is only matched by what's going on inside.

The General Staff is all there, in the Oval Office, uniforms perfectly ironed and medals hiding the cloth, but they all looked like scared children. One of them opens his mouth: “President-” “SILENCE!” the voice booms, surpassing for once the mayhem outside, then the noise returns, as all others within the room stand silently. The President is red, and he sees everything that the same color. “What are you fucking DOING?!” he screams, directed at the Chief of Staff. “We are trying to push towar-” “Trying?! You are TRYING?! We are the United States of America! We don't fucking try! We WIN! I sent an army against a CORPSE! The Pan-Africanists have nothing! How could you LOSE?!” All men lower their heads in shame. “Get out of my sight! The next time I see you, I'll get you to a court martial to see if you truly deserved them!”

As the men leave the room, the President finally looks at the papers thrown across his desk. With trembling hands, he reads them one after the other, for the tenth, no, it has to be the twentieth time. They are all there, the fucking NUMBERS. The dead in this godforsaken war, the killed in the countless riots all throughout the country, the perished in the fires and among the police, and finally, the polls. Of all these damned numbers, the polls are the only ones steadily decreasing towards zero. No, soon they'll enter the realms of the negative. He doesn't read the last report from Hoover. He already knows it.
strings.USA_africa_riots.4.a: Do something, damn it! Do! Fucking! Something!
strings.USA_africa_riots.5.desc:
President {usa_getleader} opened the last newspaper, and he would have felt relieved if not for the noise coming from outside. Finally conceding to the FBI, he had ordered a general censorship of all media, removing any and all news related to the war or the disorders, but he couldn't stop worrying: even though the New York Times had the first three pages dedicated to an extremely interesting analysis of the scientific discoveries of the last twenty years, the noise kept increasing.

It was in his head, it was in his dreams, it was in his office. The voices screamed outside the White House when he was eating, when he was sleeping, when he was working, never ceasing, never stopping, always louder. Louder. LOUDER!

“Make them stop! I don't want to hear them! MAKE THEM STOP!” He threw the newspaper away and started slamming his fists on the desk: “MAKE! THEM! STOP!”

The sudden noise alerted the secretary waiting outside. She had gotten used to the breakouts, and was immediately by his side with a glass of water: “Mister President, please, take your pills: the doctor prescribed them for your health!” and, though at first {usa_getleader} didn't seem to listen, the friendly voice slowly calmed him, until he finally agreed to take the pills, and gulped them down with the water. “Thanks, Claire...” he said in a whisper, and for a brief moment, he felt... relieved, calm, in peace.

Then the noise started again.
strings.USA_africa_riots.5.a: I beg you... please... make it stop...
strings.USA_africa_riots.6.desc:
When {usa_getleader} travelled to the Senate to ask, plead, even beg for another extension of the war measures, he had prepared for a fiery welcome, but when he stepped, for the first time in a month, outside of the White House, he realized he couldn't have prepared for what he saw.

The presidential convoy had to move incognito using civilian cars and pass through the suburbs, to avoid the riots surrounding the White House and the Senate, and through the opaque glasses the President looked at what he had done.

Houses were shut down some half-burnt, and bands of petty criminals, demagogues and political agitators from the Yockeyists and CPUSA roamed the streets now that the police was entirely occupied with preventing a total collapse of the state. Some banks had their glasses broken, general stores were heavily guarded by private security, and all the common people had the same look in their face: fear. Fear for tomorrow, fear for the lost stability, but more than anything, fear that these damn wars will claim their loved ones too.

When he descended from his car near the Senate, immediately the guards were around him, but this also made the crowd aware of his presence. Immediately, a collective roar emerged, and thousands tried to get to him: The President instinctively retreaded, scared of the hate directed towards him, while the security tried to safely get him inside the building. Then, it happened.

A single man managed to break through the shield and, before the bodyguards could get him, he slapped the President of the United States of America. Immediately, he was apprehended and handcuffed, but {usa_getleader} had felt it. In that slap, he had felt everything the entire crowd had wanted to convey him: all the hate, all the vengeance, all the pain. It was as if that man had carved his entire face with a cleaver and then filled it with salt and vinegar: he knew it, he had failed. He had failed everything and everyone. As he was finally dragged inside, and the doors closed on the noise, he couldn't stop the tears from falling.
strings.USA_you_really_fucked_up_again_DEF: the National State Of The Enclave
strings.USA_German_civil_war_category_desc:
Following the death of Führer Martin Bormann and the defeat of the German Reich in the Second West Russian War, Germany has collapsed into a devastating civil war that has effectively ended its status as a superpower for good. Such a disaster has opened a golden opportunity for the United States to cleanse Europe's soul from National Socialism once and for all - the so-called “Republic of Germany“, an official successor state to Brandt's short-lived administration residing in Berlin.

Though public support for a German government may not be popular with the American populace, covert aid in the form of arms and other military supplies may tip the scales decisively in theirs – and our – favor. All hands must be on deck in this gamble, for if Germany falls into the abyss of fascism once more, their people may never escape its grasp again.
strings.USA_AFG_WAR_sent_army_small: Send a small group of troops
strings.USA_AFG_WAR_sent_army_large: Transporting a large number of troops
strings.USA_AFG_WAR_GAS_HOLYSHIT_GAS_AFG: Gas bombs were dropped on the entire territory of Tajikistan!
strings.USA_it_time_to_end_it_all: It's time to put an end to this
strings.USA_AFG_WAR_DESC: War in Afghanistan Current Conflict Class: Level {AFG_WAR_stage}
strings.USA_GAW_Operation_Monsoon_Rain_desc: German colonial industry is heavily centralized around a handful key urban areas. We shall carry out a protracted bombing campaign to severely maim the enemy war effort.
strings.USA_GAW_Operation_Solar_Eclipse_desc: Our best planes are ready to take control of the skies. By providing a large network of defensive coverage, we ensure that our troops won't be harassed by any German planes.
strings.USA_GAW_Operation_Jackrabbit_tt: The Namibian deserts are harsh, hot, and hostile for our troops stationed in South Africa. We must prepare them for the landscape so that we can force the Sudwest out of the war.
strings.USA_GAW_Operation_Crackpot_tt: Libreville is a valuable city within the Afrikan realm, providing essential supplies to enemy troops. We need to focus our energy into an attack on this city; if we take Libreville, we damage the Zentral, and we take important resources away from the Reich's grasp.
strings.USA_GAW_Operation_Jungle_Garden_desc: The rough terrain of Ostafrika renders a land invasion nearly impossible. Luckily, we have the Rainbow Pesticides on our side. The use of these substances would clear out all the impassable foliage and make an invasion of Ostafrika much easier for our soldiers.
strings.USA_GAW_Operation_Bronze_Lion_tt: The jungles of Ostafrika provide a natural citadel for the stationed German troops. If we are to defeat the enemy, we must train our guys in jungle warfare. We need to be able to move swiftly through the trees and hit the Germans where they least expect it.
strings.USA_GAW_Intensify_Air_Support_tt: We must utilize our extensive air fleet in South Africa to provide intensified ground support actions to our troops. No kraut will be able to return fire on our lads whilst coated in napalm.
strings.USA_GAW_Helicopter_Gunships_tt: This war is rapidly proving the revolutionary utility of the helicopter in modern warfare. As helicopters are already becoming prevalent across the frontline, we may do well to attempt modification of standard crafts to carry heavy weaponry with which to provide fire support to ours and allied troops.
strings.USA_GAW_Armoured_Offensive_tt: Our military boasts a modern and capable armoured fleet, from personnel carriers to might main battle tanks that can go toe to toe with anything the krauts might field. We must utilise these to punch through the Schild lines and bring about an end to this war.
strings.USA_GAW_Heavy_Tanks_tt: We still maintain a number of heavy tanks designed to counter further advancements in heavy armour by the Unity Pakt. Should the enemy be able to deploy any such vehicles, or older models from the last war, we will be able to deploy our own tanks capable of turning them inside-out.
strings.USA_GAW_Heavy_Tanks_end_tt: A Heavy Armored Division will be deployed in DC for use in South Africa
strings.USA_GAW_Send_More_Advisors_desc: As the German war machine marches south, the free nations of the world makes their stand. We have a responsibility to protect the people of South Africa, and thus we must expand our capacity to deploy even more troops on the ground.
strings.USA_GAW_Send_Lots_Of_Advisors_desc: This war is becoming increasingly important every day that we are over here. We need to expand our logistics capabilities even more, we need to bring more troops to join the fight no matter what.
